text:
The headline is simple:

TRON now holds more USDT supply than Ethereum, with roughly $94.27B in USDT on the network.

But I think the real story is the changing role of stablecoins in the blockchain economy.

Over the past month, USDT supply on TRON reportedly increased by approximately $4B.

That's not just capital entering a token.

It's additional dollar liquidity being positioned on a settlement network.

And that distinction matters.

The first generation of crypto infrastructure was primarily designed around native assets.

Bitcoin had BTC.

Ethereum had ETH.

Other chains developed their own ecosystems around their native tokens.

But stablecoins changed the equation.

Stablecoins allow blockchain networks to carry familiar units of account across borders.

Suddenly, the most important asset on a blockchain doesn't necessarily have to be the blockchain's native token.

It can be a digital dollar.

That creates a much larger addressable market.

A trader can use USDT.

A merchant can potentially receive USDT.

A remittance user can send USDT.

A business can use USDT for settlement.

A DeFi protocol can use USDT as liquidity.

An exchange can use USDT as a base asset.

One stablecoin can therefore create demand across multiple layers of an ecosystem.

This is why the roughly $94B USDT figure on TRON deserves attention.

It indicates that TRON has become a major distribution and settlement environment for digital dollars.

And once liquidity reaches this scale, network effects become extremely powerful.

Developers want to build where the liquidity already exists.

Users want to use applications where liquidity is deepest.

Payment providers want infrastructure with established stablecoin flows.

Exchanges want networks that users already understand.

That creates a reinforcing cycle.

Liquidity attracts usage.

Usage attracts applications.

Applications attract more liquidity.

The interesting part is that this can happen without every participant being interested in TRON as a blockchain.

A user doesn't necessarily wake up thinking:

“I want to use TRON today.”

They think:

“I want to send $500.”

If the underlying infrastructure allows that transfer to happen efficiently, the blockchain becomes useful whether or not the user ever thinks about the technology underneath it.

That's how infrastructure adoption often works.

The best infrastructure eventually becomes invisible.

And stablecoins could accelerate that process dramatically.

The global financial system is still heavily fragmented.

Different countries use different banking systems.

Cross-border transfers can involve multiple intermediaries.

Settlement windows can create delays.

Fees can accumulate across the chain of intermediaries.

Blockchain-based stablecoins offer a different architecture: digital value that can move continuously across a public network.

TRON's growing USDT liquidity positions it directly inside that experiment.

This doesn't mean stablecoins will immediately replace traditional banking.

The transition is likely to be much more gradual.

But every additional dollar that becomes comfortable moving on-chain expands the potential role of blockchain settlement.

That's why I think the competition between blockchains will increasingly be measured by economic activity rather than simply transaction counts.

How much stablecoin liquidity is there?

How much value is settled?

How many users depend on the network?

How deep is the liquidity?

How many payment and financial applications connect to it?

Those metrics tell us much more about infrastructure value.

TRON's USDT position is therefore significant because it combines liquidity with utility.

$94.27B is not merely a large number sitting on a dashboard.

It's a large pool of digital dollars available to participate in an expanding on-chain economy.

And if that pool continues growing, the implications compound.

More liquidity.

More settlement.

More applications.

More financial connectivity.

More reasons for users to remain inside the ecosystem.

The most interesting part of this story may therefore come after the milestone.

What will the next $50B of stablecoin liquidity enable?

That's where the real network effect could emerge.

text:
Arsenal could have the Premier League's best midfield for Chelsea on Sunday.

Mikel Arteta joked last season about how many midfield line-ups he had on his iPad. Now he has six fit options who all offer something different.

Martin Odegaard, Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the first two games and hardly put a foot wrong.

Lewis-Skelly made 19 passes into the final third vs Coventry, then a more grown-up defensive display at Aston Villa.

Rice covered ground offensively and defensively, driving run vs Coventry led to the second goal and another vs Villa led to the Saka penalty shout.

Bruno Guimaraes could change it. Arteta said this pre-season: "He has tremendous timing and intuition to win the ball back and progress plays very fast. He's comfortable putting people through, moving between the lines."

Bruno had 4 assists at the World Cup for Brazil, was Newcastle's most progressive passer last season, and made 6 line-breaking passes in just 19 minutes at Villa Park. He found Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka with quick passes in behind in both cameos.

Then Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi. Merino completed 3 take-ons in 20 minutes at Villa, joint-second in the league for Matchday 2. Zubimendi was more combative than last season, crunching into tackles.

Chelsea have averaged 32.4% possession and conceded 5 goals, with Enzo Fernandez gone to Manchester City, Moises Caicedo injured and Lamine Camara deal failed on deadline day.

Arteta's dilemma is who plays the incisive pass and who covers the wide areas from midfield. Lewis-Skelly and Bruno both break lines. Rice covers wide areas with ease.

Sunday is best attack vs best midfield, Arteta vs Alonso, Havertz vs his former club.

Arsenal's midfield depth could be the difference this weekend.

Last week, Becky Friend, Clinical Skills Facilitator at Benenden Hospital, and Cheryl Lythgoe, Nurse Consultant and Head of the Benenden Charitable Trust, delivered Be a Lifesaver (BLS) training to non-clinical hospital teams and local businesses.  

The sessions gave participants the confidence to act in an emergency, teaching essential CPR and defibrillator skills that could one day help save a life.  The training also celebrated the Benenden Charitable Trust's donation of defibrillators to 42 UK businesses that offer corporate Benenden Health membership to their employees.  

Becky said: "80% of cardiac arrests happen at home, so Basic Life Support and CPR are life skills we should all have the chance to learn. Take the time to learn the skill, you never know when you may need to be a lifesaver."  

As a hospital rooted in the local community, we're proud to support businesses across Kent and beyond, helping more workplaces gain access to lifesaving equipment and the knowledge to use it when it matters most.

text:
To most of us, at least at a first glance, maps appear to describe reality. They show states, borders, capitals, and frontiers with the reassuring precision of geography. We learn them at school, consult them in newspapers, and rarely question the assumptions they contain. A mountain either exists or it does not, and a river follows its course. A border appears equally factual.

But maps don’t simply record the world “as it is”—they record political settlements. Every border reflects decisions made by people under particular historical circumstances, typically through wars, negotiations, or revolutions. Unlike mountains and rivers, they are neither inevitable nor permanent. They are products of history. Yet something curious happens with time. Political settlements gradually lose their appearance of contingency. What began as one solution to one historical problem or circumstance comes to be treated as reality itself, and the map appears to describe the natural order of the world.

This is not an argument against borders. Almost every political community requires them. Nor is it an argument that every territorial claim deserves recognition—most do not. The question I pose today is a different and more skeptical one: Can political settlements become so familiar that we stop asking whether they still describe political reality?

Look at a modern map of the Middle East and you will find, among many, Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria. But you will not find a state called Kurdistan. The Kurds are commonly described as one of the world’s largest stateless peoples. Estimates vary because the states in which Kurds live do not all collect ethnicity data in comparable ways. Roughly 30 to 35 million Kurds live primarily across Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria, with a large diaspora in Europe and elsewhere. They speak several closely related varieties of Kurdish, principally Kurmanji and Sorani, and have maintained a distinct cultural and historical identity for centuries. Modern Kurdish nationalism developed mainly in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Today Kurdish political life ranges from constitutional self-government in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, with its own parliament, presidency, government, universities, courts, and security institutions, to autonomous or party-led structures elsewhere. Kurdish armed forces are equally diverse: the Peshmerga serve the Kurdistan Region in Iraq, while Kurdish-led forces such as the YPG, YPJ, and later the Syrian Democratic Forces emerged during the Syrian civil war. The expression “the Kurds,” therefore, describes not a single political organization but a dispersed people living under very different political systems.

Borders and Spectrums
Long before diplomats drew the borders of the modern Middle East, Kurdish communities inhabited the mountainous region stretching across what are today south-eastern Turkey, northern Iraq, western Iran, and northern Syria. 

They spoke related languages, cultivated rich literary and oral traditions, developed local institutions, and sustained a historical memory tied to a recognizable homeland. For centuries, Kurdish communities lived within the Ottoman and Persian empires. 

These empires exercised authority unevenly, often governing through local rulers, tribal confederations, religious leaders, and hereditary principalities, rather than through a single centralized administration. Imperial rule could be harsh, arbitrary, and violent, but it often left substantial room for local institutions to manage everyday life.

As the great empires gave way to modern nation-states, governments increasingly sought a different kind of authority: one language, one educational system, one army, one bureaucracy, one national history, and one political identity. Diversity that imperial systems had often accommodated imperfectly now appeared increasingly as a problem to be solved. 

The Kurdish question emerged within this transformation, created by the encounter between an older political community and a newer model of statehood that increasingly struggled to accommodate communities whose identities did not fit neatly within its national framework.

The First World War shattered the political order that had governed much of the Middle East for centuries. As the Ottoman Empire collapsed, its territories became the subject of negotiation among the victorious powers. Across the region, peoples who had long lived under imperial rule suddenly found themselves confronting a new political language: national self-determination.

" Once the new borders gained international recognition, they acquired legal authority and, consequently, a presumption of permanence."

For the Kurds, this appeared to offer an unprecedented opportunity. Kurdish representatives argued that they constituted a distinct people with their own historical homeland and therefore deserved political recognition within the emerging international order. 

They were not alone in making such claims. Armenians, Arabs, Zionists, Persians, and other communities and governments were also advancing claims about sovereignty, mandates, borders, national government, or self-determination as the Ottoman order was dismantled.

But Kurds faced a particular disadvantage. Unlike several neighbouring national movements, they possessed neither a unified government nor a single diplomatic leadership capable of speaking for all Kurdish regions. 

Their political reality exceeded their level of political organization. Among the most prominent Kurdish advocates was Şerif Pasha, a former Ottoman diplomat who presented a memorandum on Kurdish claims to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919. Acting as a leading Kurdish representative in Paris, he argued for recognition of a Kurdish political homeland in the post-Ottoman settlement, and submitted maps and territorial claims intended to give the Kurdish case diplomatic form. 

His position did not represent every Kurdish leader or region, but it was one of the clearest attempts to place Kurdish self-determination before the victorious powers in formal international diplomacy.

In 1920, the Treaty of Sèvres recognized, at least in principle, the possibility of Kurdish autonomy and, under certain conditions, eventual independence in parts of the former Ottoman Empire. 

The treaty settled almost nothing, but it briefly established that the international order at the time acknowledged a Kurdish political future as conceivable. Barely three years later, that possibility disappeared.

Military victories by the Turkish nationalist movement transformed the diplomatic landscape. In 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne replaced Sèvres, recognized the sovereignty of the new Turkish Republic, and abandoned the earlier provisions concerning Kurdish autonomy.

By the mid-1920s, the basic framework had been set. The Ottoman Empire was gone. The Republic of Turkey had been recognized. Iraq had been constructed under British influence with Mosul included. Syria had been placed under French mandate. Iran continued its own centralizing state project.

 Kurdistan was divided among Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria. The Kurds did not move. The borders moved over them. A Kurd in Turkey now faced one state, one army, one ideology, one school system, one prison system, one legal vocabulary. A Kurd in Iraq faced another. A Kurd in Iran another. A Kurd in Syria yet another.

Once the new borders gained international recognition, they acquired legal authority and, consequently, a presumption of permanence. Questions that had recently belonged to international diplomacy were reclassified as domestic affairs. Kurdish demands for self-government were no longer debates about the political order of the Middle East. They became internal problems for the states that governed Kurdish populations.

In Turkey, Kurdishness was long treated as a defect in the project of one Turkish nation. 

The republic presented itself as modern, secular, civilizing, and unified. Kurdish language, memory, and self-rule appeared as backwardness or a threat to national unity. In Iraq, Britain acknowledged Kurdish distinctiveness when useful, then subordinated Kurdish self-rule when it interfered with the Iraq it wanted to build.

 Later Iraqi regimes, especially the Baathist state, would take this contradiction to catastrophic extremes through Arabization, village destruction, chemical attacks, and the genocidal Anfal campaign.

" Maps don’t simply record the world “as it is”—they record political settlements. Every border reflects decisions made by people under particular historical circumstances. "

In Iran, Kurdish leaders negotiated, organized, or declared self-rule in moments of state fragility, only to face execution or repression once Tehran regained strength. 

Iranian state forms changed—Qajar, Pahlavi, Islamic Republic—but Kurdish self-rule was repeatedly treated as a threat to central authority.

 In Syria, denial often worked more quietly. It operated through language restrictions, Arabization, and administrative erasure. 

Many Kurds in Syria were rendered stateless after the 1962 census. Kurdish identity was made faint in public life, not always through spectacular massacre, but through the slow violence of non-recognition.

This shift profoundly altered the burden of justification. 
Now, those seeking to change the (newly) established borders had to explain and advocate why they should be changed. 

The question was no longer What political arrangement best reflects the peoples of the region? but rather How can political aspirations be accommodated without disturbing the existing map?

If the Kurdish question were simply the story of a people denied a state, its history would read like a sequence of unrelated defeats and occasional victories. 
One rebellion follows another. One uprising succeeds briefly before being crushed. 
One generation places its hopes in diplomacy, another in armed struggle, another in constitutional politics. 

Look more closely, however, and you’ll notice that Kurdish self-government has often advanced when central governments were weak or when outside powers provided protection, only to become vulnerable when the regional balance of power changed.

Brief Experiments in Kurdish Statehood

The collapse of the Ottoman Empire created several opportunities for Kurdish self-government, although none produced a durable state. 

One of the first arose around Sulaymaniyah, in what is now the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. After the First World War, British authorities appointed Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji, an influential religious and tribal leader, as governor of the area. 

He soon sought greater independence from British control and led an uprising in 1919.

After a period of imprisonment and exile, he returned to Sulaymaniyah and in 1922 assumed the title King of Kurdistan. 

His authority extended over a relatively small territory and depended heavily on religious standing, tribal alliances, and personal loyalty. British and Iraqi forces eventually ended the experiment. 

It was a limited and politically fragile precursor to modern Kurdish nationalism, but it established an early precedent for Kurdish attempts to turn the collapse of Ottoman rule into political sovereignty.

A more developed experiment appeared in north-western Iran after the Second World War. 

The Republic of Mahabad was proclaimed in January 1946 under Qazi Muhammad, leader of the newly established Kurdish Democratic Party.

 The republic established a government and promoted Kurdish-language education, publishing, and political organization. 

Its emergence was closely connected to the Soviet occupation of northern Iran, however, and Soviet military and economic support was important to its survival. 
When Soviet forces withdrew in 1946, the republic lost its principal external protection. Iranian forces reoccupied Mahabad in December, and Qazi Muhammad was executed in March 1947.

The most durable Kurdish political project began in Kurdistan after the 1991 Iraq Gulf War.

 Kurds rebelled against Saddam Hussein’s government, and the regime’s counteroffensive produced a mass exodus toward Turkey and Iran.

 The international response included Operation Provide Comfort, a security zone in northern Iraq, and restrictions on Iraqi military aircraft. These measures helped create an area beyond Baghdad’s effective control in which Kurdish political institutions could develop.

" Kurdish identity was made faint in public life, not always through spectacular massacre, but through the slow violence of non-recognition."

In May 1992, Kurds in Iraq held parliamentary elections and established a regional legislature and government. The political system was imperfect from the beginning. 

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) dominated political life, and their rivalry developed into armed conflict in the mid-1990s. 

The two parties effectively governed separate zones until a U.S.-brokered agreement in 1998 helped end the fighting. Nevertheless, the Kurdish administration survived and gradually developed into a durable regional government.

The overthrow of Saddam Hussein in 2003 strengthened its legal position. Iraq’s 2005 Constitution formally recognized the Kurdistan Region and its existing authorities as a federal region. 

Kurdish self-government was therefore incorporated into the constitutional structure of the new Iraqi state rather than existing solely through foreign protection or Baghdad’s weakness. 

Over more than three decades of substantially autonomous Kurdish government in Kurdistan in Iraq, the Kurds have demonstrated the ability to administer territory, maintain public institutions, conduct elections, provide security, and negotiate with foreign governments over an extended period.

Another Kurdish-led political system emerged during the Syrian civil war. Beginning in 2012, as Syrian government forces withdrew from much of the north, the Democratic Union Party (PYD) and its armed forces, the YPG and YPJ, established control over several predominantly Kurdish areas. 

These territories later developed into a broader autonomous administration encompassing Kurdish, Arab, Assyrian, and other communities. 

The governing project, commonly associated with the Kurdish name Rojava, placed unusual emphasis on decentralized administration, political participation of women, and multi-ethnic representation.

The rise of the Islamic State in 2014 gave Kurdish forces a much larger military role. ISIS captured Mosul, conquered large areas of Iraq and Syria, and carried out a genocidal campaign against the Yazidis of Sinjar. The Kurdish response was not uniform.

 Peshmerga units, the armed forces of Iraq’s autonomous Kurdistan Region, withdrew from much of Sinjar as ISIS advanced in August 2014, leaving Yazidi communities exposed to mass killing, enslavement, and forced displacement. 

Syrian Kurdish YPG fighters and forces associated with the Turkey-based Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) subsequently helped establish an escape route from Mount Sinjar. Kurdish forces in both Iraq and Syria then became increasingly important in the wider campaign against ISIS.

In Syria, the YPG and YPJ played a central role in the defense of Kobani, and the later Syrian Democratic Forces became the principal local partner of the U.S.-led coalition in much of the campaign against ISIS. In Iraq, Peshmerga forces fought alongside Iraqi and coalition forces across a long front.

 The war demonstrated that Kurdish institutions were capable of fielding organized military forces and cooperating extensively with Western governments even in the absence of an independent Kurdish state.

That experience contributed to the Kurdistan Regional Government’s decision to hold an independence referendum on September 25, 2017. The ballot covered the recognized Kurdistan Region as well as disputed territories then under Kurdish control, including Kirkuk. 

According to the regional electoral commission, 92.73 percent of participating voters supported independence, with turnout above 70 percent. The size of the majority provided unusually clear evidence of support for statehood among those who voted, although the inclusion of disputed territories made the referendum more contentious.

The referendum had little international backing. Iraq rejected it as unconstitutional. Turkey and Iran, both of which have large Kurdish populations of their own, strongly opposed it. 

The United States also opposed holding the vote at that time, arguing that it could destabilize Iraq and complicate the final stages of the war against ISIS. The United Nations likewise warned against a unilateral referendum.

The stronger contemporary case rests on self-determination and demonstrated political capacity.

The consequences came quickly. In October 2017, Iraqi federal forces moved into Kirkuk and other disputed territories that Kurdish forces had controlled since the collapse of the Iraqi army in 2014. 

Divisions between the two main Iraqi Kurdish political parties, the KDP and PUK, contributed to the rapid Kurdish withdrawal. 

The referendum therefore produced an unusual result: an overwhelming vote for independence followed almost immediately by a reduction in Kurdish territorial and political leverage.

These episodes form an important part of the modern case for Kurdish statehood. 

They show repeated attempts to establish political institutions across several parts of the Kurdish-populated Middle East, as well as sustained popular support for self-government.

Kurdish-majority territory remains divided among four existing countries; many of the areas claimed by Kurdish nationalists contain substantial Arab, Turkmen, Assyrian, Armenian, Yazidi, and other populations.

Institutions and Governing Capacity

Past persecution supplies only part of the argument for Kurdish statehood. The stronger contemporary case rests on self-determination and demonstrated political capacity. 

The Kurdistan Region in Iraq in particular has functioned as a largely self-governing political entity since 1991 and as a constitutionally recognized federal region since 2005. Its institutions have serious deficiencies, but they have also endured for more than three decades. 

The 2017 referendum showed that independence has broad support among its electorate. Whether those facts justify changing Iraq’s borders is ultimately a political and moral judgment.

The Kurds have repeatedly shown they can establish institutions when the geopolitical space allows. Sheikh Mahmud’s short-lived government around Sulaymaniyah combined personal, religious, tribal, and administrative authority, but remained narrow and fragile.

 The Republic of Mahabad went further, creating a government, political administration, Kurdish-language education, publishing, and organized national institutions before Iranian forces reoccupied the area.

After 1991, the Kurdistan Region in Iraq developed the most durable example: parliamentary elections in 1992 produced an elected legislature, a regional government, and a judicial council; after 2005 these institutions, as well as universities, gained formal recognition within Iraq’s federal constitution.

 In Rojava (Syria), Kurdish-led authorities developed local councils, civilian administrations, security forces, and other institutions we commonly associate with modern governance, including gender parity and multiethnic participation.

These relatively recent experiments with Kurdish statehood in Iraq and Syria do not prove that a future Kurdistan would necessarily be democratic, but they do show that Kurdish political life has already produced institutional experiments that can be evaluated, criticized, and improved rather than dismissed as purely hypothetical.

Khaled Salih -----  is Emeritus Vice-Chancellor of the University of Kurdistan Hewlêr, where he served from 2012 to 2016. 
He was a Visiting Researcher in Political Science at the University of Pennsylvania in 2011, adviser to the Kurdistan Regional Government from 2003 to 2010, and a lecturer at the University of Southern Denmark’s Center for Middle Eastern Studies from 1997 to 2003. 

His new book is When Parochial Error Goes Global: Islam, Epistemological Closure, and the Defense of the Open Society.

📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        September 4, 1870

France has lost its Emperor at Sedan. A republic is proclaimed from from the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. The new government calls itself the Government of National Defence and immediately discovers that none of Europe's great powers intend to defend it. Thiers is making political tours in the hope of gaining support, but it is the outcome of military action that leads to peace.

Napoleon III surrendered at Sedan along with more than 100,000 French soldiers, 413 field guns, and 139 fortress cannons. The Emperor himself taken prisoner on the battlefield. Two days later, on September 4, republican deputies Gambetta and Favre led a crowd to the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. The Third Republic was proclaimed. General Trochu became its president; Favre its foreign minister; Gambetta its minister of the interior.

Russia's chancellor Gorchakov advised the new French government to make peace as quickly as possible. He promised that the Tsar would write to Wilhelm I recommending "moderation." He added that if a European congress were convened, Russia would "raise its voice loudly" in France's favour.

When the French chargé showed Gorchakov a draft telegram containing the phrase "Russia will not permit a peace that violates our territorial integrity," Gorchakov stopped him immediately: "Not to permit something means for a great power to take up arms to prevent it. Russia cannot go that far." 

On September 12, Adolphe Thiers, Foreign Minister in the new government, set out on a diplomatic mission to the capitals of the great powers on behalf of the Government of National Defence. He visited London, Vienna, St Petersburg, and Florence, seeking either intervention on France's behalf or mediation toward an acceptable peace.

In London, Gladstone's government received him warmly and did nothing. The British were content to watch France - their main rival as a colonial and naval power - be weakened. They had, in any case, already secured from both belligerents in August a reaffirmation of Belgian neutrality, which was their primary concern. In Vienna, Austria-Hungary refused any active intervention outright. Italy gave the same answer.

In St Petersburg, the Tsar expressed his desire for peace and promised to facilitate negotiations, "but not more," Gorchakov told Thiers. The Tsar did write a new letter to Wilhelm. The Prussian response was a long time coming. When it finally arrived, Gorchakov summoned Thiers and told him that "peace is possible." He indicated he considered the peace terms Prussia would offer to be acceptable. 

The diplomatic tour failed to change the military situation. But it unsettled Bismarck. He feared foreign intervention (from Russia most of all) and pressed the Prussian military command to finish Paris quickly, demanding merciless bombardment and growing angry with Moltke for the lack of siege artillery.

Meanwhile Gambetta, operating from Tours after escaping the siege of Paris by balloon on October 7, was raising new armies in the provinces with extraordinary energy. Prussia found itself tied down before Paris with one half of its forces and engaged against Gambetta's new armies with the other. The situation was becoming uncomfortable.

On October 27 Marshal Bazaine surrendered Metz and his entire army (173,000 men) to the Prussians. The forces previously besieging Metz were now free to act against Gambetta. On January 28, 1871, the Government of National Defence signed an armistice.

The Third Republic that began on September 4, 1870 would last until 1940 — when Germany came back.

AWCN COURSE 10/2026 PARTICIPANTS COMMENCE OPERATIONAL THEATRE VISIT TO 1 DIVISION

Participants of the Army War College Nigeria (AWCN) Course 10/2026 have officially commenced an operational theatre visit to the Headquarters of the 1 Division, Nigerian Army, and Operation FANSAN YAMMA in Kaduna. Led by the Team Leader, Brigadier General John Mbanefo, the delegation arrived for the exercise which began at the First Division Auditorium on September 3, 2026.

The strategic visit is designed to bridge the gap between classroom theory and real-world application, deepening the participants’ practical understanding of contemporary military operations, operational art, and campaign planning as part of their higher military education.

Welcoming the delegation, the General Officer Commanding (GOC), 1 Division Nigerian Army, and Commander, Sector 1 Joint Task Force, Operation FANSAN YAMMA, Major General Abubakar Sadique Muhammed Wase, described the tour as both timely and vital.

Major General Wase, who was represented by the Commander of the 51 Signal Brigade, Brigadier General Opeyemi Olusegun Okungbure, underscored the volatile and evolving security dynamics within the Division’s Area of Responsibility.

He highlighted 1 Division’s pivotal role in the broader North-West security framework, emphasizing its responsibility in securing critical transit corridors that connect the North-West zone to neighboring states and other regions of the country. Specifically, he noted that the Abuja–Kaduna highway remains a critical artery for national security and economic activities, serving as a lifeline to both the North-West and North-East.

Brigadier General Okungbure challenged the participants to fully immerse themselves in the field experience by engaging directly with commanders and troops, analyzing operational realities on the ground, and extracting actionable lessons to improve future campaign planning and overall combat effectiveness.

Reiterating the value of the exercise, the Team Leader, Brigadier General John Mbanefo, stated that the theatre visit offers an invaluable environment for participants to study ongoing operations through the lens of operational art. During the tour, participants will evaluate existing contingency plans, review current operations, and analyze how operational estimates are translated into successful field execution. He noted that assessing the decision-making patterns and intelligence infrastructure used by field commanders is central to mastering modern military campaigning.

Earlier in the program, the Team Coordinator and AWCN faculty member, Colonel Jerry Maigari, provided an overview of the institution's mission. Established in 2017, the Army War College Nigeria is dedicated to grooming highly educated, innovative, and professional operational-level leaders for the Nigerian Army.

Colonel Maigari disclosed that Course 10/2026 comprises 100 distinguished middle-to-senior level officers. This includes 89 Nigerian officers and 11 allied participants drawn from Ghana, Botswana, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Cameroon, Chad, Guinea, and South Africa. He added that local and international study tours remain a cornerstone of the college's curriculum, with the Kaduna leg explicitly tailored to unpack the complexities of Operation FANSAN YAMMA.

The operational theatre visit is expected to reinforce the critical link between professional military education and the fluid demands of safeguarding Nigeria’s strategic environment.

AJEMASU YAKE JINGINA
Lieutenant Colonel
Acting Deputy Director Army Public Relations
1 Division Nigerian Army/Sector 1 Operation FANSAN YAMMA 
3 September 2026

text:
There is just one problem with this quote.

Krishna never says it to Shakuni in Vyasa’s Mahabharata.

Not in K.M. Ganguli. Not in the Critical Edition.

“Deceit in the service of Dharma is Dharma” may make a terrific meme.

It is not Vyasa.

Nor does Krishna tell Shakuni that the Pandavas must “win by any means” or that Bhishma, Drona and Karna will all be killed through deceit.

What the Mahabharata actually gives us is far more disturbing.

When Drona is tearing through the Pandava army, Krishna does advocate deceiving him about Ashwatthama. But listen to what he actually says:

अस्मिन् काले अनृतं सत्यतो विशिष्यते
“In this situation, falsehood is superior to truth.”

And he immediately grounds it in the saving of life.
That is not a blank cheque for deceit.

Then comes Karna.
His wheel sinks. He gets down. 

Suddenly, he appeals to dharma and asks Arjuna to observe the rules.
Krishna’s answer is savage.

Now you remember dharma?
Where was that dharma when Draupadi was humiliated?
Where was it when Yudhishthira was cheated?
And where was it when Abhimanyu - Arjuna’s son, Subhadra’s son, Krishna’s own nephew was surrounded and killed?

Krishna does not offer us the cheap maxim:
“The end justifies the means.”

Vyasa forces us into something infinitely harder:

What does Dharma do when Adharma breaks the rules and then invokes those very rules when it needs their protection?

And it is infinitely more unsettling than the meme.

text:
The MIT economist Barack Obama called into the White House to model the Affordable Care Act accidentally destroyed the pricing consulting industry in a free 76-minute lecture on the math behind every price on earth.

He filmed the lecture as part of MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics and it has been on OpenCourseWare ever since.

McKinsey partners charge Fortune 500 CEOs $500,000 a day to teach a diluted version of what he covers in 76 minutes for free.

His name is Jonathan Gruber. He is the Ford Professor of Economics at MIT and one of the two economists Obama's team called into the White House in early 2009 to model the cost curve of the Affordable Care Act.

The 76-minute clip in this video is one lecture from 14.01, walking a room of undergraduates through the equation called price elasticity of demand.

The whole framework fits on a napkin.

Elasticity equals the percent change in how many people buy divided by the percent change in your price.
If the number is bigger than one, your product is a luxury and raising the price will kill your revenue.
If the number is smaller than one, your product is a necessity and raising the price will grow your revenue.
Necessities like gas, medicine, and bread are inelastic. Luxuries like restaurants, Netflix, and brand-name coffee are elastic.
Never set a price without first estimating this number for your customers.

That single equation is what every insurance company, oil producer, and streaming service on earth uses to decide the price of what they sell to you.

It is also the math behind the worst timing mistakes in markets.

When a stock, a fund, or an AI-driven strategy falls, most investors treat it like a luxury. Demand collapses. They sell.
When the same asset rips higher, they treat it like a necessity. Demand explodes. They chase.

The price moved.
Their elasticity moved more.

"Elasticity is the great secret of economic life."

That is Alfred Marshall, the Cambridge economist who invented the concept in 1890. Gruber returns to the sentence in every version of the course. Almost no founder pricing a product, employee negotiating a raise, or landlord setting a rent has ever asked for the elasticity of their own offer.

Almost no investor has asked for the elasticity of their own behavior.

Every hedge fund on Wall Street pays $250,000-a-year analysts to estimate demand elasticity on the fly. Every retail consumer is the price-taker on the other side of the equation.

The lecture is free on MIT OpenCourseWare. Gruber's textbook is under sixty dollars.

Almost none of the millions who watched have ever calculated the elasticity of their own product, salary, rent, or next panic sell.

The math is free.
The edge is estimating the elasticity of your own decisions before the next forecast, model update, or drawdown talks you out of compounding.

Genetically modified pig kidney functions for record 271 days in US man

A genetically modified pig kidney functioned in a US man for 271 days, setting a record for the longest time a pig kidney has operated in a human body, according to the Punch.

Tim Andrews, 66, received the kidney at Massachusetts General Hospital in January 2025 after developing end-stage kidney disease linked to type 2 diabetes. The transplant freed him from dialysis while he awaited a human donor.

The kidney initially worked immediately, but doctors removed it in October after blood-vessel damage, inflammation and eventual failure. Andrews subsequently spent 82 days on dialysis before receiving a human kidney in January 2026.

Researchers said the pig had undergone genetic modifications to improve compatibility and reduce immune rejection. They said xenotransplantation could offer hope to patients facing the shortage of human donor organs.

Then they built the loans around it.

Islam forbids riba, interest. So cities, states, and federal housing giants did not tell people to use the same loans everyone else uses. They rewrote the product so it would comply with Islamic law.

Start in Minneapolis.
In 2006 the City Council approved an Alternative Financing program. It launched in 2007. The city’s own site says it “conforms with Islamic law.” Ordinary city loans charge 2% interest. This version charges a 2% “rate of return” so the borrower does not pay interest.

A private lender puts up half. The city matches the rest with public money, now up to $75,000. Since launch, Minneapolis has issued about $1.44 million through that program to 48 businesses.

That is not a private bank being “inclusive.” That is taxpayer cash structured to Sharia.

It is not only Minneapolis.
Louisville rewrote its small-business lending so METCO could offer a “Sharia-compliant modification option.”
Philadelphia’s housing plan called for developing a “Sharia-compliant Financing Product.”
Seattle’s mayor’s office created an action item: “Housing Tools for Sharia-Compliant Lending.”
Maine changed the rules so state-chartered credit unions can offer Sharia-compliant mortgages.

Minnesota’s Department of Revenue even published tax instructions for “Shariah Compliant” home financing, cost-plus-profit instead of principal-plus-interest.

Then look at the federal housing machine.
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are government-sponsored enterprises. After 2008 they were bailed out and put in federal conservatorship. They buy mortgages so lenders can keep making more loans. That pipeline is backstopped by the U.S. government.

In 1997–99 the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said Islamic lease-to-own structures could be treated like regular home loans. Guidance Residential, the largest U.S. Islamic home financier, has put more than $10 billion into 40,000-plus homes. It sells those co-ownership contracts into Freddie Mac. That is how a religious no-interest product scales in America: government-backed liquidity.
They will tell you it is just “faith-friendly banking” and open to anyone. Fine. Then why did city halls and federal housing giants specially design the paperwork around riba?

Christians, Jews, and everyone else pay interest on a normal loan or they don’t borrow. One group got cities and Fannie and Freddie to rebuild the product so Sharia is satisfied.
If government will change lending for Sharia, it will change the next rule too.

Your money. Their law. Our country still has one Constitution.
One law. No parallel finance system paid for by the public.

Beachgoers

Boating

•Gulf Stream: West wall relatively close in (recent data: ~7 nm east of Port Everglades, ~15 nm NNE of Fowey Rocks). Northward flow typical; no major hazards.

Fishing/Diving

•Visibility & Conditions: Fair to good nearshore with ~2 ft seas. Best clarity during slack tides. Storm chances present through the afternoon.

•Practical Tips: Slack periods ideal for diving. Fish early or late to avoid heat and storms. Gulf Stream edges productive offshore.

Righteous Allegiance by George Yuhasz

A divided nation. A deadly plot. A man caught between two worlds.

Will Manley is a rising star in the U.S. Government’s clandestine services—an undercover agent tasked with stopping a domestic terror group bent on reshaping America. But as he immerses himself in their radical ideology, he faces a battle more personal than he ever anticipated: a choice between his government career and the legacy of his Native American roots.

At the heart of the struggle is Elias McArdle, a brilliant and ruthless former U.S. Army commander. FBI agent Ron Shortridge works to unravel a web of hate and hidden agendas before an act of terror changes the country forever. Meanwhile, Lenape elder Rebecca Hurney offers a path of healing through ancient wisdom—but time is running out. And a mysterious red fox, secretive and resourceful, may be more than he appears to be.

Filled with suspense, mystery, and political intrigue, *Righteous Allegiance* is a gripping thriller with complex characters that will appeal to fans of Vince Flynn, Lee Child, and Tom Clancy.

text:
#OTR | Iran–Oman Hormuz Framework Offers a Corridor, Not Yet a Glut

A joint Iran–Oman statement dated 1 August 2026 sets out a phased plan to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz: a temporary joint maritime corridor, a joint mine-clearance project, and further talks on a permanent corridor, traffic management and information exchange, with other Gulf coastal states to be brought in. The text stresses sovereignty and international law. It is a diplomatic opening, not a reopening.

Markets will treat it as a risk-reduction signal, not as restored Qatari and UAE volumes. Gulf LNG losses of around 45% year-on-year still leave 2026 trade roughly flat only because US, African and Australian cargoes filled the gap. A usable corridor would ease TTF/JKM tightness and pull the delayed surplus closer to 2028; a corridor that exists only on paper keeps Atlantic Basin and African spot barrels in demand.

Africa sits on both sides of any thaw. Nigeria, Tortue, Congo FLNG and Mozambique remain swing suppliers while Hormuz is impaired. Egypt, Senegal and prospective South African and Ghanaian import projects need cheaper cargoes if LNG is to displace diesel in power. A credible clearance timetable would compress the import bill; a stalled one keeps fiscal pressure on buyers and keeps only lower-cost African export projects bankable.

The statement matters because logistics, not resource size, now set the price. Until mines are cleared and a corridor is used, not merely proposed, the glut stays postponed and African FID decisions still turn on offtake, fiscal terms and country risk.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. The implications stretch far beyond individual dating lives and directly into how psychological fidelity is defined in the digital age. Couples are already clashing over virtual attachments, while tech companies aggressively monetize loneliness without providing any meaningful ethical guardrails for consumers.

We are rapidly heading toward a future where emotional exclusivity will no longer be limited strictly to human partners, forcing society to rewrite the rules of love and commitment.

text:
TWO FOLD FI is offering quite an innovative combo DEX + liquidity provision + yeild earning platform. 

It's kind of a mix of everything right now: swap between tokens, deposit ISDG or WETH for higher than market yeild or stake $TWO for yeild. 

The platform uses Uniswap v4 hooks to keep USDG deposits in a loan pool while pulling out only the exact liquidity needed for swaps, earning fees from both lending and swapping. 

Of note here is there are serious returns to be had for staking your $TWO tokens over at @twofoldfi a platform that earns depositors yeild

HOW DOES IT WORK:

Taken directly from the docs:

--------

""The idea fits in one sentence: LP capital rests in a lending vault and steps into the pool only for the instant a swap needs it, so a liquidity provider collects both income streams on the same dollars."

"A Twofold pool is an ordinary Uniswap v4 pool with the hook attached. 25 of them are open, listed on the Registry, and readable by anyone: one WETH pair, one TWO pair, one USDG/USDe stable pair, and the rest tokenized equities against USDG."

--------

This is an innovative use of v4 hooks that brings something new to the table here. Protocol revenue feeds back to the token. In fact, you have two options as the token holder to stake into vault 1 or vault 2:

Vault 1: stake $TWO and receive $TWO. Right now the APY is crazy high. It's about 600%. I hope this gets turned down because this kind of inflation, without any counter, will just lead to a price decline as stakers sell.

Vault 2: stake $TWO, earn USDG from the protocol; earnings from the swap fees + lending fees go to the stakers. I have not tested the APY in this pool, so I can't comment on it, but it's listed as even higher than Vault 1 at about ~650%

Huge returns here to be had. I am in Vault 1 there with my staked tokens, and in half a day, I'm earning $400 USD! That's close to 1,000 USD per day paid out in claimable $TWO tokens. Crazy! It reminds me of the 2020 defi days where you would stake your token (or eth) in a newly launched protocal and earn 500% paid back in tokens...

Downsides: huge inflation from the token. A big chunk of the supply is given out as staking rewards. In fact, the staking rewards are ludicrously high right now: 600%-700% APY for just staking your $TWO tokens.

Now, I'm not sure what the long-term unique value play is for @twofoldfi here. The project appears to be more of a wrapper for a v4 hook, something that can potentially be replicated elsewhere. So right now, this seems like a good short-term user-acquisition move to get attention and TVL to the site (for the rewards), but the pressure will be to offer MORE on top of this.

Offering 2020 levels of 'paid in ecosystem token by staking the same token' ends up crashing the token economy.  For a quick growth hack, yes, but anything mid- to long-term, they need to replace this with something more sustainable.

One option being remove the staking rewards in $TWO, burn that extra supply (or most of it), and convert some of the USDG fees into buyback and burn. The addition of OTHER services on the platform (once people come to earn yeild or use the swap), offer more services and more ways to earn fees. Maybe going in the direction of an aggregator rather than just a DEX (too competitive).

SUMMARY 

I'm waiting to see what the future plans are. For now, it's quite impressive, showing from a UX standpoint and a tech demo of u4 hooks used to enhance yields.

Deposit USDG and start earning. Hold the token if you wish to bet on future platform growth, and earn a huge amount of the token or share in the protocol fees.

I'm not quite sure WHAT the site is trying to be, though:

Is it trying to be a DEX?

Is it trying to be a liquidity provider?

Is it trying to be an aggregator for swaps?

Is it trying to be a yield generator for stables?

So I would like to see future expansions. For now, it's a yeild platform. I do feel there is a serious growth story if they can add more services here. I'm holding a bag, and I actually bought back 80% of the position I sold around 1.5M for at 2x the price, so I have a good bet that they can do this.

Don't search for “remote jobs.”

Search for:

“async remote” “no meetings” “written communication” “flexible hours” “independent contributor” “results-based”

A remote job can still have 6 hours of meetings every day.

National Macadamia Nut Day🌰🧆🤎🍪🌰⚪️🥜✨😋

National Macadamia Nut Day, celebrated on September 4th, marks a special occasion to honor a nut that’s not only delicious but also packed with history.

Originating from Australia, macadamia nuts were discovered by the native Aboriginal people and introduced to the European settlers in the 19th century. Named after John Macadam by Ferdinand von Mueller, a German-Australian chemist, these nuts found their way to Hawaii in the 1880s.

There, they were initially used to protect sugar cane from the wind. However, their cultivation soon took off, and by the mid-20th century, macadamia nuts had become a global sensation​​​​​​​​.

Growing macadamia nuts is time-consuming and labor-intensive. This contributes to their status as one of the most expensive nuts in the world. It can take up to ten years for the trees to produce their first crop, but once mature, they are capable of producing nuts for over a century.

This slow cultivation process, coupled with their rich, buttery flavor, has made macadamia nuts a luxurious and sought-after ingredient in various culinary applications, from baking to cooking and snacking​​.

National Macadamia Nut Day provides a perfect opportunity for food enthusiasts and nut lovers alike to indulge in and celebrate the unique taste and texture of macadamia nuts.

Whether enjoyed roasted, salted, or coated in chocolate, these nuts offer a blend of flavor and versatility unmatched by many.

text:
Not-So-Typical Millennial(s)
by Greg Allen
Published Sep 15, 2016 

I met Amber, 20, and Luke, 19, at a bookstore recently.  They’re from a small Hoosier town near the Ohio border and they were gracious enough to give me their take on a few questions I posed.

Millennials seem to get a bad rap.  Although no two individuals are alike, the general consensus is Millennials are lazy, uninformed, and they think they’re entitled.  How do you debunk that stereotype?

Amber ~ “I think it all starts at home.  My parents are my role models and they instilled in me morals and the value of hard work.  I’m constantly humbled by what I have been blessed with.  It’s a pretty embarrassing stereotype, but I do not feel I should be identified simply by the generation in which I was born, but rather by my actions and personality.”

Luke ~ “Although I do not support stereotypes or prejudice, there is usually a sliver of truth behind them.  We are seen as lazy, uninformed, and we think we are special and entitled.  From where does this description arise?  Sadly, it’s from our actions and it’s something we need to work on.”

What’s your take on the 2016 Presidential Election?

Amber ~ “I think this is an election like none before.  Donald Trump is a very outspoken man.  This can be both beneficial in the sense of relating to the American public, by not being a typical politician, but it has also gotten him in trouble because he doesn’t put a filter on first.  As for Hillary Clinton, the biggest hold back would be the controversy regarding the confidential emails to her personal devices and her deletion of them.  I think it will be difficult for Americans to back someone who has committed such crimes against their country.”

Luke ~ “We have reached the point where it seems like nobody is voting for someone, but everybody is voting against someone else.  This is tragic, because it means that we do not have a candidate that anybody actually wants or trusts to be our next President of the United States.”

Do you think a lack of respect plagues many Millennials?  If so, where do the roots of this degenerative attitude come from?

Amber ~ “I think the roots of this degenerative attitude comes from our increased use of social media.  It’s a lot easier to make rude comments when you are typing it on a computer screen rather than having to look the person in the eyes.  We are more often occupied by the virtual people on the screen than by the real people sitting across the dinner table from us.”

Luke ~ “There were rebels that showed disrespect in other generations.  I think disrespect plagues my generation just as much as it does any other.”

Your parents generation are called “Baby Boomers,” and your grandparents are called “The Greatest Generation.”  What’s your take on those individuals?

Amber ~ “I have mowed my Grandparents’ lawn for ten years and always plan time to spend talking with them afterwards and drink the root beer they never forget to offer.  This summer was different.  It was filled with stories from my grandfather who recounted the times he went down to Texas to pick cotton and the very first night of his honeymoon and my grandmother got homesick.  It was during these times that I suddenly realized I knew very little about the people I loved.  I could not be more thankful for the Parents God has blessed me with.  I definitely attribute my character and values to being molded by my Parents.”

Luke ~ “As I see it, ‘The Greatest Generation’ probably criticized ‘The Baby Boomers’ for being lazy, uninformed, and thinking they’re special and entitled.  Now, ‘The Baby Boomers’ are criticizing us.  It’s a vicious cycle.”

Has technology been a blessing or curse to Millennials?  Has that technology blurred personal and social skills in individuals?

Amber ~ “I see technology as being both a blessing and a curse.  I substitute teach in my hometown and I understand teachers want to incorporate the positive aspects of technology as learning mechanisms, but some days I feel like I‘m just moving kids from one screen to the next and they’re losing the interaction with others and learning the social skills that will be needed later on in life to be successful.”

Luke ~ “We’re all moving towards a more technological age; we just need to be smart about it and use it responsibly.”

Patriotism is generally steeped in history.  Are such things of interest to you?

Amber ~ ”Patriotism is of great interest to me, and I would hope to my generation as a whole.  I believe it’s very important that we understand that God is our leader.  I read on a church sign recently, ‘In order for a nation to get back on her feet, her people need to get down on their knees.’  That resonated with me.  Patriotism involves being proud of who you are and the nation that you are a part of.”

Luke ~ “I find history and government fascinating.  However, there is always more to learn and I think that these are subjects that all Americans should know more about.”

As an American, what’s important to you?

Amber ~ “Freedom is the first word that comes to mind.  It’s important to me that people are reminded that freedom isn’t free.  My brother is currently serving our country.  I think Americans take for granted the tremendous amount of freedoms and blessings we have as a country.  Our ancestors journeyed many miles from what was familiar and fought many battles to establish the amazing country that we have today.”

Luke ~ “Trying to secure ‘The American Dream.’”

What would you like my readers to know?

Amber ~ “There are many occasions where I wish I had grown up in the 60s or 70s with less technology and more written letters and late nights playing cards with friends and family.”

Luke ~ “Let us be who we are.”

Greg Allen’s column, Thinkin’ Out Loud, was published bi-monthly from 2009 to 2017.  He’s an author, a former nationally syndicated columnist and the founder of Builder of the Spirit Ministries in Jamestown, Indiana.  He can be reached at https://t.co/9QdchPfdBy.

1. Verses that mention meat / hunting
These are the main passages people cite. Animals named are boar, deer, antelope 
Ayodhya Kanda 2.52.102 — after crossing the Ganga, hungry:
तौ तत्र हत्वा चतुरो महामृगान्
वराहमृश्यं पृषतं महारुरुम् ।
आदाय मेध्यं त्वरितं बुभुक्षितौ
वासाय काले ययतुर्वनस्पतिम् ॥

Rama and Lakshmana, famished (bubhukṣitau), killed (hatvā) four large animals: wild boar (varāha), white-footed antelope (ṛśya), spotted deer (pṛṣata), and a great ruru stag. They took the pure/edible portion (ādāya medhyam) and went to a tree for the night.

Ayodhya Kanda 2.96.1–2 — at Chitrakuta, with Sita:

निषसाद गिरिप्रस्थे सीतां मांसेन छन्दयन्
इदं मेध्यमिदं स्वादु निष्टप्तमिदमग्निना ।
Rama sits on the hillside gratifying Sita with māṃsa (flesh/meat) and says: “This is medhya (pure/fit), this is tasty, this is roasted in fire.”
Ayodhya Kanda 2.56 (around 22–34) — settling the hermitage: Rama asks for aiṇeya māṃsa (antelope venison) for the vāstu rite. Lakshmana kills a black antelope (kṛṣṇa-mṛga), cooks it until it is heated through and bloodless (niṣṭaptam chinna-śoṇitam), then they offer cooked meat with fruits and roots. “Blood drained / limbs cooked” is hard to read as fruit pulp.
Aranya Kanda 3.47.22–23 — Sita to the disguised Ravana:

She says her husband will return after killing ruru deer, godhā (monitor lizard), and boars, bringing plenty of āmiṣa (meat). That is how she describes ordinary forest food.
Aranya Kanda 3.68.32–33 — funeral offering for Jatayu:
Rama cuts rohi-māṃsāni (deer flesh) into balls (peśī-kṛtvā) and offers them as piṇḍa. That is a funeral rite, not a picnic — but it still uses the word for flesh.
Sita’s vow to Ganga (2.52.89): after returning to Ayodhya she will worship Ganga with a thousand pots of surā and māṃsabhūta-odana (rice mixed with meat).

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Legendary author Cormac McCarthy wrote every single one of his acclaimed novels, including Blood Meridian, No Country for Old Men, and The Road, on a cheap, manual Olivetti Lettera 32 typewriter he bought at a pawn shop in 1963 for $50.

​For nearly 50 years, McCarthy typed roughly 5 million words on the exact same portable machine without ever using a computer or word processor. He maintained the typewriter himself, blowing out dust with an air hose at service stations and replacing the ribbon whenever it wore out.

​In 2009, when the machine finally began breaking down beyond repair, his friend Ole Christensen bought him a replacement model for $20. McCarthy then sent his original $50 typewriter to auction at Christie's to benefit the Santa Fe Institute. Bidders expected it to fetch around $20,000, but it sold for a staggering $254,500.

More Surprising Facts About Cormac McCarthy:

A. ​He Lived in Extreme Poverty by Choice: Early in his career, McCarthy refused commercial offers to give paid lectures, write journalism, or teach university classes, preferring total poverty so he could focus purely on writing. His second wife, Anne DeLisle, recalled living in a barn with no indoor plumbing or hot water in Tennessee, bathing in a creek because he turned down $2,000 speaking gigs.

B. ​He Preferred Scientists Over Other Writers: McCarthy detested literary circles and rarely hung out with other authors. Instead, he spent the last several decades of his life as a trustee and resident scholar at the Santa Fe Institute, a theoretical science research facility. He spent his days eating lunch with quantum physicists, evolutionary biologists, and mathematicians, even editing their academic papers for fun.

C. ​A Notorious Hatred for Quotation Marks: McCarthy famously refused to use quotation marks in his books, calling them "clutter." He believed that if prose was written clearly enough, the reader wouldn't need punctuation marks to know who was speaking, limiting his punctuation almost exclusively to periods, commas, and capital letters.

D. ​The Inspiration Behind The Road: The idea for his Pulitzer Prize–winning post-apocalyptic novel The Road struck him in 2003 while visiting El Paso, Texas, with his young son, John. Looking out over the city at 2:00 AM, he imagined what the fires and mountains might look like 50 to 100 years in the future, writing down a few notes that sat untouched until he expanded them into the book years later.

SUMMARILY! 
​From hammering out literary masterpieces on a $50 pawnshop typewriter to rejecting commercial wealth in favor of living in a barn and hanging out with quantum physicists, Cormac McCarthy approached his life and art with ruthless, singular dedication.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

The Medic Who Writes™🌚

A setback can feel like ruin, yet the sudden turn in the road may have kept you from something worse. McCarthy does not make hardship noble. He treats it as a possible shield against a fate you never saw coming—and a reminder that survival, in a hard world, often arrives in ways no one would choose.
