text:
"Handshaking Distance"

Forrest, Morton, and the one command that still fought artillery at rifle range

It was the afternoon of June 10, 1864, and the road out of Brice's Crossroads was narrow, and dry, and about to become famous. Four Confederate field pieces came down it at a gallop. They did not stop at a respectful distance and begin their business the way the manuals said a battery should. They came inside two hundred yards of a Federal infantry line, wheeled, and unlimbered in the open. Then, in a war where guns had learned to fear rifles, they did something rifles were supposed to have made impossible. They opened with double-shotted canister at point-blank range, and held their ground while the enemy came on.

In one of the stands that followed, the Federals closed to fifty yards. Captain John W. Morton, twenty-three years old and in command of those guns, would later put it in words that needed no embellishment: the enemy came, he wrote, "almost within handshaking distance of our guns." His crews did not run. They changed projectiles, double-charged the tubes, fired, and held. The line in front of them broke.

That is not how Civil War artillery was supposed to work by 1864. It is not how it usually did work. The men responsible were Nathan Bedford Forrest and his young chief of artillery, and together they were the exception that makes the rule visible.

How the guns were supposed to fight

American field artillery came into 1861 still carrying the habits of Mexico. In that earlier war the light batteries had rolled to just outside smoothbore musket range, call it two hundred yards, and blown gaps in the enemy line with canister so the infantry could go through and finish the work. A 6-pounder or a 12-pounder howitzer could do this because the men waiting on the other side of the field could not answer effectively much beyond seventy-five or a hundred yards. Canister was the killing round. Everything else the piece could fire - shot, shell, spherical case -was what a gunner used while he was still working his way close enough to use canister.

The early war still looked like Mexico on some fields. Batteries unlimbered boldly, right up under the enemy's nose, because the officers commanding them had learned their trade under Taylor and Scott and expected the guns to go forward with the attack, the way the guns always had. First Bull Run. Wilson's Creek. The early hours at Shiloh, before the fighting had taught its first hard lessons. Pieces sat closer to the enemy than any late-war artilleryman would have tolerated, and got away with it, because the rifle-musket, though it was already in the armies that first summer, had not yet reached enough hands, and not enough of the hands that held it yet understood the sights.

The inherited rule was simple enough to fit on a recruiting poster: get to canister range, wreck the formation, limber up and run if the infantry comes on before you're done. The new rifle made the first half of that sentence expensive. It made the second half urgent.

What changed between 1862 and 1863

Two things happened at once, and they did not happen on the same clock in every theater, which is part of why the story is so easy to oversimplify.

The rifle-musket filled up the line first. Neither government could put a Springfield or an Enfield in every soldier's hands in the first year of the war: there were not enough rifles, and there was not yet the industrial machinery behind either army to make enough of them fast. By late 1862 the process was well along in Virginia. By the middle of 1863 it was the rule in both major armies rather than the exception. Stonewall Jackson's Second Corps still carried a mongrel mix of weapons in the winter of 1862 and 1863 - .69 caliber smoothbores next to .54 caliber rifles next to .58 caliber rifle-muskets, whatever a man's regiment happened to have drawn. After Chancellorsville the same corps had been sorted down to a single caliber. The pattern repeated itself across both armies through 1863: battlefield captures, foreign imports run through the blockade, and growing domestic production finally put into the ordinary soldier's hands the weapon the range charts had been advertising all along.

The second change mattered more, and it is the one modern readers tend to miss. The men who could actually use that extra range were pulled out of the main line and put in front of it. From early in the war the flank companies had gone forward as skirmishers, and those companies got the first rifles when rifles were still scarce, since it made sense to arm the men already doing the long-range work. By 1863 the Army of Northern Virginia was building whole sharpshooter battalions at the brigade level. The Army of the Potomac and the western Federal armies thickened their own skirmish lines, and later handed some of those skirmishers breechloaders that could put three or four rounds downrange to a rifle-musket's one. You did not need an entire regiment of men capable of estimating six hundred yards by eye. You needed one company willing to lie down in the grass, pick out a horse, and shoot it.

That is the distinction that matters more than the simple fact that both armies now carried rifles. A battery going into action against a division of 1864 infantry was not facing only the main line at a hundred yards, the way its Mexican War ancestors had. It was facing a skirmish line that could begin killing the battery's horses at four to six hundred yards, long before the guns were even in position to answer, and a main line waiting to finish whatever the skirmishers had started. The horses were always the real target. It was the horses, not the gunners, that decided whether a battery left a field with its pieces or left them behind in the mud. The accounts from both sides say the same thing so often it stops sounding like an accident: the gunners were still serving their piece when the account breaks off. The teams were down. The battery was finished.

By the middle of the war the standard answer was not to charge the guns to sixty yards and trust to nerve. It was to unlimber farther back, work the tubes with shell and case shot, hold canister in reserve for the moment the enemy actually reached the gun line, and accept, because there was no honest way around accepting it, that the old offensive charge of Mexican War artillery had become one of the more reliable ways to lose a battery outright. This did not drive the guns from the field. It drove them out of the business of leading the assault, and into the business of breaking one that had already begun.

John Pelham is the comparison that makes the difference visible. Pelham took his guns forward -famously so at Fredericksburg, where a single gun under his hand delayed a Federal advance that outnumbered him by more than a hundred to one - but he fought from defilade, from a flank, shifting one piece at a time under counter-battery fire to buy a few more minutes for infantry that needed them. That is aggressive horse artillery, and it is deservedly remembered as such. It is not four guns galloping down an open road into the enemy's front, as the spearhead of a dismounted charge, to fire double canister at whatever stood in the way. Pelham harassed, and delayed, and bought time with a single piece cleverly placed.

Forrest and Morton did not delay anything. They finished it.

The exception

Morton himself refused the credit history was ready to hand him. In the history he wrote in 1909, he was plain about it: the idea that artillery could be fought "at as close range as rifles" was not his invention. He claimed only that he understood what Forrest wanted, and did it. Many of the orders he received, he admitted without apology, existed nowhere in any tactics manual either army issued. He carried them out anyway, because the man who gave them was Forrest.

The pattern held from Parker's Crossroads through Brice's Crossroads, through the hard pursuits that followed, through Athens and Sulphur Trestle and Johnsonville. Forrest put his guns in front of his dismounted troopers. He sent them down the road with the attack itself, not behind it. He walked them into a defilade so tight that even Forrest, on at least one occasion, first said the position and the enemy's gunboats together would knock the pieces to splinters - and then changed his mind, and went ahead anyway.

At Brice's Crossroads the sequence is the cleanest example the war has to offer, and it is worth walking through slowly, because everything that made the method work is visible in these few hours.

The batteries made an eighteen-mile approach over roads that were bad even by the standards of a Mississippi June, and they went into action behind Forrest's first line, the way artillery was supposed to fight in 1864. That much was orthodox. Late in the afternoon, with the Federal infantry already wavering under the pressure Forrest's dismounted men had been building all day, Forrest told Morton to load four of his eight guns with double canister and stand ready at the limber. When the bugle sounded, Morton was to take the pieces as close to the enemy as the ground would allow, and - in the phrase Forrest actually used, and that Morton never forgot — "give 'em hell."

Morton's own letter home, written only a few days later, is blunter than anything that made it into the official reports. He charged with the batteries nine separate times that afternoon. At one point two of his pieces stood twenty or thirty yards in front of his own infantry line - ahead of the men who were supposed to be protecting them. The enemy closed to fifty yards. Morton's crews switched to double canister and fired two volleys, then three more, and then went forward with the guns themselves, into the wreck of the Federal line, yelling as they came.

After the break, Morton kept the guns moving on the heels of the retreating Federals all the way through the disaster at Tishomingo Creek, where Sturgis's column, already beaten, came apart entirely trying to cross a single bridge under fire. Forrest rode beside him through the pursuit, telling him to "keep the skeer on 'em, John." Later, Forrest told him something else, in fewer words, and meant it as the simple truth: the guns had won the battle.

That is Napoleonic close support, fought in 1864, in a war whose ordinary practice had already abandoned it as a form of slow suicide.

Why it worked anyway

It did not work because the rifle-musket had somehow forgotten how to kill a horse at four hundred yards. It worked because Forrest almost never asked his guns to do what a corps battery in Virginia was required to do on a normal Tuesday.

He chose his fights. Brice's Crossroads was a meeting engagement against a Federal column that had marched hard over bad roads in bad heat, and Sturgis's infantry arrived blown, strung out, and half a step behind its own cavalry. That is not Hancock's line waiting patient and entrenched on Cemetery Ridge. It is not a veteran Federal division that has spent the whole morning improving its works, with a skirmish line already out and settled at four hundred yards, watching the approaches with rifles zeroed. Forrest picked his moment, and his moment was rarely that one.

He built the conditions before the guns ever closed. The artillery charge, in Forrest's hands, was the last act of the play, not the first. Dismounted troopers went in ahead of the guns. A flank gave way, or was made to give way. The particular pressure Forrest called "the skeer" - the sense, spreading through a line under attack, that the attack was not going to stop - came first, and only then did the guns arrive to finish what the skeer had already started. Double canister at sixty to two hundred yards against a line that is already looking back over its shoulder for the road home is a different tactical problem than the same canister fired into the teeth of a fresh, confident, veteran regiment that knows exactly how far three hundred yards is because someone has drilled it into them.

The guns themselves were few, and light, and did not have to be husbanded for tomorrow's set-piece battle the way a massed Federal or Confederate artillery reserve did. Morton typically fought with four to eight pieces: 3-inch rifles the command called "Rodmans," 12-pound howitzers, 6-pounders, never the kind of consolidated battalion that an army commander had to preserve intact for the next campaign. Forrest treated captured Federal guns as a renewable resource, replacing what he lost from what the enemy left behind. No conventional army in either government could have accepted the loss rate in horses that this kind of fighting demanded. Forrest could, because he was not fighting the same war they were.

Two of the guns that made the method possible were not ordinary battery pieces at all, though they looked it. Morton and Forrest called them Rodmans, and the name stuck, because the tubes resembled the standard 3-inch Ordnance Rifle closely enough that nobody thought to ask twice. They were not Ordnance Rifles. They were two of only six 3-inch cast-steel rifles ever made - cast in 1862 by Singer, Nimick & Company of Pittsburgh, serial numbers 1 and 5, eight hundred and thirty-four pounds apiece - and they had been captured at Lexington, Tennessee, on December 18, 1862, a gift the Federal government had not intended to make. A wrought-iron Ordnance Rifle had a deeper voice when it fired. These barked. The battery took to calling them the Bull Pups, and Forrest said, more than once, that he feared no attack at all so long as Morton and those two guns were somewhere on the field with him. A command built around galloping its artillery to canister range needed pieces that could actually keep up with the horses. These could. That was not a small thing. It may have been the thing.

He gave the order himself, every time, and then rode with the guns to see it carried out. A Federal battery commander in the Army of the Potomac who took it upon himself to run four Napoleons to sixty yards without being told to would have spent the rest of his career answering for it, assuming he lived long enough to answer for anything. Morton never had to answer for it, because Forrest had told him to do it, and Forrest was standing there when he did. At Johnsonville the two of them were both on the elevating screws together, adjusting the guns by hand.

The enemy's posture mattered as much as anything else on this list. Forrest went after cavalry first when he could get it, and infantry that had not yet finished deploying when he couldn't. When the method was carried into a more conventional fight, under a different commander who did not share Forrest's instincts for it - at Harrisburg (Tupelo), where S. D. Lee dispersed the guns in the orthodox pattern of individual support rather than massing them the way Morton wanted - the result was ordinary. Unremarkable. The kind of fight the tactics manuals had actually been written for.

The risk calculus, in the end, was simply different for Forrest than for anyone else holding a similar rank in either army. He would spend an entire battery to break a column in a single Mississippi afternoon, and count it a fair trade. An army that had to fight the same enemy again on the same ground the following week could not make that trade and expect to still have an army. That is not romance, however much it reads like it on the page. It is accounting. Forrest simply kept a different set of books than the men around him, and for a handful of afternoons in Mississippi and Tennessee, the books balanced.

**************************************************
General Nathan Bedford Forrest; Captain John Watson Morton, Forrest's Chief of Artillery; Singer-Nimick cast steel "Bull Pup" one of Morton's original two

text:
The One Chatham Vision: A discussion with Dr. Kelly Batten - 9.3.26

👤 New superintendent: Dr. Kelly Batten became superintendent of Chatham County Schools on July 1 after 14 years with the district, most recently serving as assistant superintendent for human resources.
🎓 Experienced educator: Batten previously worked on early college programs, advanced coursework and professional development in Chatham County. Earlier, he was principal of Carver High School, held leadership positions in Wake County Public Schools and began his career as a high school social studies teacher.
🤝 Relationships matter: Batten said one of Chatham County Schools’ defining strengths is its emphasis on relationships among students, staff, families and the broader community.
📈 Virginia Cross Elementary highlighted: Batten pointed to Virginia Cross Elementary as a statewide example of student growth, saying the school has exceeded state-predicted outcomes for six consecutive years and has drawn a visit from State Superintendent Mo Green.
🏆 National recognition for teachers: Pittsboro Elementary teacher Shane Henderson was recently named a Milken Educator Award winner, one of about 30 educators selected nationally. Batten noted that Chatham Central’s Eric Patton previously received the honor.
🎯 Teaching and learning remain the priority: Batten said the district’s central mission is to remain “laser focused on high-quality teaching and learning,” arguing that successful schools strengthen businesses, nonprofits and the broader community.
🏥 Student success extends beyond classrooms: Looking at countywide data, Batten emphasized that health care, infant mortality, housing and residential mobility can affect whether children arrive at school prepared to learn and thrive.
🎓 Dual-enrollment opportunities are a major strength: Chatham County Schools’ partnership with Central Carolina Community College allows students, in some cases beginning in 10th grade, to earn college credit at no cost while still attending high school.
💼 College credit can improve opportunities: Batten said dual-credit courses can strengthen students’ competitiveness for college admission, scholarships and employment while reducing the time and expense required to earn a degree.
📊 District tracks students over time: Rather than relying exclusively on a single year’s test results, Chatham County Schools follows student cohorts to examine academic progress from elementary school through graduation.
🎓 Graduation rate reaches 92.2%: Batten announced that the district’s latest graduation rate is 92.2%, presenting it as an important measure of long-term student success.
📚 Third-grade reading shows improvement: Batten said 85.5% of Chatham County third-graders can demonstrate reading proficiency when the state’s additional approved measures of proficiency are considered alongside end-of-grade testing.
🗺️ One Chatham strategic plan approaching renewal: The district’s current One Chatham strategic plan runs from 2022 through 2027. Batten confirmed that another strategic-planning cycle will follow.
🏫 Safe schools will remain a strategic goal: Batten said maintaining safe, welcoming school environments will continue to be a priority because students must feel secure and supported before effective learning can occur.
👩‍🏫 Teacher retention is a major objective: The district has set a goal of retaining at least 90% of its staff despite an increasingly competitive education labor market.
🎁 Community helps welcome new employees: About 80 new employees joined the district in August and received welcome packages supported by local organizations and businesses, an effort Batten said demonstrates that the community values educators.
🏠 Housing affordability threatens recruitment: Batten identified Chatham County’s rising cost of living as one of his biggest workforce concerns. Teacher salaries are largely determined by the state salary schedule, which has not necessarily kept pace with local housing costs.
💵 Local supplements help but do not solve the problem: Chatham County remains among the state’s leaders in local salary supplements for school employees, according to Batten, but those supplements have not fully offset the county’s increasing cost of living.
🚗 More employees commute into Chatham: Because of affordability pressures, increasing numbers of school employees live in Alamance, Wake and other neighboring counties. Batten warned that commuters may eventually take jobs closer to their homes.
🏗️ Growth requires flexibility: With Chatham County potentially changing significantly during the next five to 10 years, Batten said the school system must remain flexible in its facilities, curriculum, workforce and strategic planning.
🚘 VinFast offers a planning lesson: Batten cited earlier discussions about creating educational programs connected to VinFast as an example of why the district cannot assume today's economic-development projects will determine tomorrow's workforce needs.
🏭 County economy has transformed: Batten noted that manufacturing companies dominated Chatham County’s largest employers around 1990, while the county's employment base became more diverse in subsequent decades.
👨‍💼 Schools are Chatham County's largest employer: Chatham County Schools currently represents the county’s largest employer, giving the district an important economic role in addition to its educational mission.
🌱 Keeping graduates in Chatham is a long-term challenge: Batten said economic development should create opportunities that allow more Chatham County students to build careers and lives locally instead of having to leave the county for employment.
🤝 Businesses can become stronger school partners: Batten encouraged companies to examine their existing relationships with schools and identify ways to support students, families and employees that fit each business's capabilities and values.
🔄 Partnership should work both ways: He stressed that school-business relationships should not simply consist of the district asking businesses for money or assistance; partnerships should create meaningful benefits and connections across the community.
💰 Schools also contribute indirectly to the economy: Although the district is not a revenue-generating business, Batten noted that its employees and families support local stores, restaurants, gas stations and other businesses.
📣 District is “open for business”: Batten invited business and community leaders interested in deeper partnerships to connect directly with district officials, including community-relations staff, to develop new opportunities.
🧭 Overall message: Batten presented Chatham County Schools’ next chapter as centered on academic achievement, teacher recruitment and retention, affordability, strategic flexibility, community partnerships and preparing students for a rapidly changing county.

text:
01. A $200 Wake-Up Call: The Myth of the Monolithic Agent

A developer recently voiced their frustration on X:

"Burned through 86% of the weekly Grok @bot limit on the $200 Ultra plan in just 1.5 days! Anyone else experiencing this or am I doing something wrong? I wasn't even using it that heavily..."

This isn't an isolated incident. From indie builders to enterprise engineering teams, anyone experimenting with autonomous coding agents has faced the same "bill shock": hundreds of dollars burned in tokens, thousands of context queries wasted, yet the actual task remains half-baked or broken.

Most people assume they just wrote poor prompts or blame model providers for aggressive rate limits. But the root issue lies much deeper: the entire industry's mental model for building and using AI agents has been fundamentally flawed.

02. The Trap of the "Black-Box God Agent": A Runaway Token Incinerator

Today, the predominant paradigm for AI agents is simple yet disastrous: dump a massive, ambiguous end-to-end task into a single LLM and pray that it magically solves everything in a black box.

When an agent is forced to act as a monolithic general solver, it inevitably breaks down:

Hallucinatory Loops & Endless Rabbit Holes: The agent guesses blindly, querying massive dumps of irrelevant documentation, wandering down false assumptions, and looping endlessly on errors.
Exponential Token & Compute Waste: Large Language Models are probabilistic prediction engines. Using expensive, non-deterministic probability models to guess what deterministic code should execute is burning dollar bills to heat a room.
Zero Production Viability: No serious enterprise can deploy a workflow with unpredictable run costs, non-reproducible outcomes, and zero determinism.

Expecting a single LLM to handle everything is like manufacturing a modern automobile and demanding that not only the driver, but the engine pistons, transmission gears, and every single screw must have sentient thoughts. It is not just absurd—it is an architectural failure.

03. The Screw Analogy: LLMs as Orchestrators, Standard Programs as Screws

To make autonomous agents reliable, scalable, and cost-effective, we must return to a fundamental law of software and industrial engineering: separation of concerns and deterministic execution.

"Even in a fully AI-powered future, you cannot turn the screws into AI. Standard programs are the screws of the digital age. Top-level interaction and decomposition belong to LLMs; bottom-level execution must strictly belong to deterministic programs."

The Screws: Deterministic Standard Programs
File I/O, compilation, linting, API calls, database queries, and test runners have been perfected across decades of computer science. They offer 100% determinism, sub-millisecond execution, and exactly zero token cost. They are precision components that should never be replaced with probabilistic guesses.
The Orchestrator: Large Language Models (Specialized Agents)
The true genius of LLMs lies not in brute-force manual labor, but in understanding human intent, breaking ambiguous goals into structured sub-tasks, and orchestrating deterministic tools at key decision points.

The hygienic execution loop is straightforward:
Human defines the goal ➔ LLM parses intent and decomposes the task ➔ Deterministic standard tools execute the atomic steps ➔ Predictable results are verified ➔ LLM synthesizes progress and reports back to the human.

04. How Grix Solves This: Multi-Agent Orchestration with Standard Tools

In the open-source collaboration platform Grix, this layered architecture is built directly into the foundation:

Role Isolation & Clean Boundaries:
Instead of a bloated "do-everything" agent, Grix separates responsibilities into distinct specialist agents (e.g., Coder, Tester, Docs, Ops), each with dedicated context and tight scopes.
Deterministic Tool Integration:
Agents interface with local developer environments, CLI utilities, and standard scripts via clean protocols—delegating deterministic jobs to deterministic code.
Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Messenger Interface:
By bringing humans and multiple agents into a familiar WeChat/Slack-style group chat, developers retain full visibility and authorization control. Tasks remain inspectable, pauseable, and immediately actionable from mobile and desktop alike.

05. Moving from AI Craftsmanship to Industrial Engineering

The goal of artificial intelligence is not to discard decades of proven software engineering, but to give those battle-tested tools an intelligent, communicative orchestrator.

Stop trying to make screws out of LLMs. Let models orchestrate, let standard code execute, and let human-agent teams collaborate with total transparency—that is the only sustainable path to production-grade AI.

text:
Our Lady of Consolation is a title given to the Virgin Mary, also known as Comforter of the Afflicted. It presents her as a mother who draws near to those in sorrow and offers the comfort that comes through her Son.

The title has deep roots in Augustinian tradition. According to that tradition, Mary appeared to Saint Monica while Monica grieved the death of her husband and the wayward life of her son Augustine. Mary gave her a leather belt, or cincture, as a visible sign of her presence and protection. Monica wore it from that day and later recommended it to Augustine after his conversion. The belt became a distinctive part of the Augustinian habit and the basis for a confraternity that spread the devotion among both religious and lay people. In this light Mary is seen as especially close to those who need companionship and encouragement.

A separate and equally ancient strand of the devotion centers on Turin. Tradition holds that an icon of the Virgin, sometimes said to have been painted by Saint Luke, was brought from the East by Saint Eusebius and given to Saint Maximus, the first bishop of Turin, in the fourth or fifth century. The image was hidden during later turmoil and later recovered in 1104 after a blind pilgrim from France received a vision directing him to the ruins of an old chapel. When the icon was unearthed, the pilgrim’s sight was restored. The shrine that grew around the image, known as La Consolata, became a place of pilgrimage, and the city of Turin later took Our Lady of Consolation as its patroness.

In the seventeenth century the same title took on new life in Luxembourg. During years of war, plague, and famine a Jesuit priest carried a wooden statue of Mary and the Child in procession. The statue was later placed in a chapel outside the city walls and soon attracted pilgrims who reported healings and other favors. Our Lady of Consolation was named patroness first of the city and then of the entire duchy.

The title itself appears in the Litany of Loreto as Consolatrix Afflictorum. It expresses a simple theological conviction: Jesus is the consolation of the world, and Mary, who stood at the foot of the Cross and was herself comforted by the hope of the Resurrection, now consoles those who suffer. Shrines dedicated to her under this name arose in many places, including Carey, Ohio, where a replica of the Luxembourg statue arrived in 1875, and West Grinstead in England. Across these sites the same figure is honored: not a distant queen, but a mother who stays with her children in their affliction and points them toward the source of true comfort.

text:
Sandhill Cranes Adapt to Area’s Changing Landscape, Officials Say🪶🌳

If you’ve lived in Lake or Sumter County for any length of time, chances are you’ve stopped your car for a sandhill crane.

Whether they’re wandering through neighborhoods, strolling across golf courses or calmly leading their gangly youngsters across a busy road, the towering birds have become one of the region’s most recognizable residents.

While many people assume development pushes wildlife farther away, Florida’s resident sandhill cranes have learned to live alongside people in surprising ways.

That doesn’t mean development has been entirely beneficial.

According to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), Florida is home to two subspecies of sandhill cranes. While greater sandhill cranes migrate to Florida each winter before returning north to breed, Florida sandhill cranes live here year-round.

Their natural habitat includes open prairies, pastures and freshwater wetlands, but they have also adapted to developed areas that offer similar features.

“Florida sandhill cranes can be found in urban and suburban areas that have features similar to their natural habitat, including open settings, particularly mowed grass, water features and food sources such as earthworms, mole crickets and turf grubs,” says Lisa Thompson, communications specialist for FWC’s Division of Habitat and Species Conservation.

“That’s why you may see Florida sandhill cranes using golf courses, suburban neighborhoods and even airports for foraging and, in some cases, nesting.”

The same landscapes that provide food and open space also create new dangers.

text:
The sequence you describe is the part of Lutnick’s account that has drawn the most scrutiny, because his own earlier public statements and later testimony sit uneasily together.
In a 2025 podcast interview, Lutnick said that after the 2005 townhouse visit—when Epstein made the massage-table comment he found “gross” and “disgusting”—he and his wife decided he would “never be in the room with that disgusting person ever again.” He added that he was never in a room with Epstein socially, for business, or for philanthropy after that.42
Seven years later, in December 2012 (four years after Epstein’s 2008 Florida conviction), emails show Lutnick initiating contact: he wrote to “Jeff” that his group (himself, his wife, their four children, another family with four children, and staff) was arriving in St. Thomas on a boat and asked for the exact location so they could meet for dinner or lunch. Epstein’s side invited them to Little St. James. Lutnick’s wife followed up confirming the large party. A follow-up note from Epstein after the visit said “Nice seeing you.” A photo from the files shows Lutnick on the island with Epstein.36
When asked under oath why they went, Lutnick testified he could not recall. He called the invitation “unsettling and inexplicable” because Epstein’s staff somehow knew his family was nearby on vacation. He described the lunch as brief (about an hour), outdoors, with roughly 15–16 people including children and nannies, after which they left. He maintained he saw nothing inappropriate and still considers all three in-person encounters “meaningless and inconsequential.” In later testimony he parsed his earlier “never in the room” statement as applying only to himself personally, not to family events.50
That is the full documented explanation Lutnick has given. He has not offered a more specific reason for accepting the invitation or bringing his children and another family’s children after the 2005 reaction. Critics, including some members of the House Oversight Committee, have called the gap between the 2005 vow and the 2012 family trip inconsistent with his earlier characterization of having cut ties. Lutnick has denied any deeper relationship or knowledge of Epstein’s crimes.

text:
One hundred forty years ago, on September 4, 1886, Geronimo surrendered to United States military forces under the command of General Nelson Miles at a place called "Skeleton Canyon," in the Arizona territory.  This action effectively ended the conflicts that had come to be known as "The Indian Wars."

Geronimo was a high-level spiritual leader and "medicine man" of the Apache nation, and six months earlier, in March of 1886, he and his band of warriors were trapped by troops led by General George Crook, and he was expected to surrender — however, he and some 40 warriors escaped the trap under cover of darkness.  The small band was then pursued by a reported 3,000 Mexican troops, and 5,000 American troops (about 1/4 of the entire United States military), and forced into the Peloncillo Mountains — even so, the band of Indians was able to fend off the joint military action for more than five months, before Geronimo offered to surrender.

Geronimo (whose name translates to English as "the one who yawns") was then transported to Fort Sill in the Oklahoma territory, where he was held as a prisoner-of-war until his death of pneumonia in 1909.  He was permitted to leave the fort from time to time (World's Fair, Presidential Inauguration, etc.), but always under strict and heavy military guard.

According to a nephew who was present at Geronimo's death, some of the final words he spoke were, "I should never have surrendered. I should have fought until I was the last man alive."

text: I was stranded there once due to the weather. Had an IT contract with Nissan, days before common internet access that could have just pushed out the update. Stick a floppy disk into a pc in the dealership and update some software. 2 dealers a day and bunch of us had the country divided up, i had Kent and Surrey. Odd out of the way places were at the end of the schedule. I got the IOM. Fly out of Heathrow in the morning, back in the evening. Stuck the car in the short stay car park, bright sunshine and really hot. Plane almost didnt land due to fog at IOM. Got down and caught a bus to the dealer, did the task in  about ten minutes and made my way back. No flights as weather so bad. Did get offered a plane share with Jasper Carrott and Rick Wakeman who had managed to find a private plane to take them to Liverpool as they had shows that day or next to get back to in North Wales and they were looking to spread the cost, but as no extra cash on me (had no CC cards then)  i couldnt take up the offer plus i really needed to get to Heathrow. Eventually everyone was given various places to stay overnight, i got a local pub with rooms, it was party night with DJ and dancing so a fun night. Next day still no planes. Eventually the weather cleared enough to get a flight early afternoon and had to pay extra for the car park. Got it all back on expenses but for a 10 minute job it was a bit of a journey for 24 hours.

text:
Pamela Schwerdt arrived as joint head gardener at Sissinghurst in 1959 and helped push its flowering season into autumn.
A friend asked me about the two younger women in this Sissinghurst photograph. One is Pamela; the other is Sibylle Kreutzberger, her fellow Waterperry-trained gardener. (That changed how I read the photograph.)

When Vita Sackville-West offered Pamela the head gardener’s post, Pamela made one thing clear: Sibylle came too. When they visited in mid-July, Vita felt the season was already over. They treated that as a challenge, using annuals and tender perennials to keep colour going into autumn and sharing the planting decisions for the next 31 years.

Sissinghurst is rightly tied to Vita’s vision, but the garden visitors came to know also owes a great deal to the two women who kept testing and extending it after her. Their approach influenced planting far beyond Kent.

text:
Do not accentuate the negative going further...

Here are at least 25 positives to blare until November:

1. He made the border a real border again. In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration. America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”   Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens. Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.  Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years. According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.  This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.  Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.  Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.  Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments. That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.   No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade. Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America. Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.  Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year. For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.  Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.  Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.  Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.  Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.   In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government. USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.  Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years. From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.  What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government. Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.  He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.  Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.  He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.  No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy. The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.  Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.  That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination. Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.  He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.  Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean. China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.  Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population. Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.  Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.  Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.  Now Act Like It Matters  Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.  Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.  And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.  Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.  This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.

UConn was one of two research schools in the US to even offer a Robotics Engineering major.

Meanwhile Connecticut just put a robot dog on the floor of a manufacturing forum in Hartford and wrote a $4.8 million check so high school kids can keep building combat bots.

China shipped ~15,000 humanoids this year. Fewer than 10% of last year’s units actually went to work.

The gap isn’t who can make a robot sprint 9.39 seconds. It’s who can keep a machine useful after the battery on the other one dies.

That’s the boring part UConn’s labs actually study. It’s also the part that pays.

• Price: 79,414 (RSI 52.4)
• Mid-term floor: MA99 at 77,359
• Range boundaries: 76,264 support / 82,300 resistance
• MA25 (78,712) acting as immediate pivot

Im sick to death of the lies regarding building in E1 of Judea and Samaria.
  
1. The master planning designations for E1—connecting the settlement of Ma'ale Adumim to Jerusalem have been legally intact within Israeli administrative frameworks since  1994.

🚨 THIS DEVELOPMENT  IS NOT  THE IMPEDIMENT TO A 2 STATE SOLUTION.  

PALESTINIAN  REJECTIONISM IS.

The historical record of Palestinian leadership and political factions declining peace proposals, partition plans, and diplomatic compromises from 1947 onward includes several key inflection points.

●1947 – UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181):  Arabs REJECTED the UN plan to divide Mandatory Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states, Jews accepted the plan.

●1948 Arab-Israeli War, Arabs rejected the State of Israel, demanding a single Arab state.

●1967 – The Khartoum Resolution: While an pan-Arab declaration rather than a uniquely Palestinian one, the PLO heavily supported the "Three No's" issued in Sudan following the Six-Day War: 
1. No peace with Israel
2. No recognition of Israel 3. No negotiations with Israel.

●2000 – The Camp David Summit: PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat rejected an offer by Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and brokered by US President Bill Clinton. The offer included a demilitarized Palestinian state encompassing roughly

Arafat declined without presenting a formal counter-proposal.

●2001 – The Taba Talks: Building on Camp David, negotiators came closer to an agreement with enhanced territorial offers, but talks were officially called off amid the ongoing violence of the Second Intifada.

94% of the West Bank (with land swaps to make up the remaining 6%), international custodianship over Jerusalem's holy sites, and a safe-passage corridor to Gaza. Abbas Rejected

●2014 – Kerry Peace Initiative: US Secretary of State John Kerry attempted to establish a framework for final status negotiations. The framework stalled when Mahmoud Abbas failed to even respond to a proposed outline presented by US President Barack Obama at the White House.

●2020 – The Trump Peace Plan ("Peace to Prosperity"): The Palestinian Authority boycotted the US-led economic workshop in Bahrain and completely rejected the subsequent political framework.
