text:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) (PART B) Tahutmes I set up his statue on the Euphrates, and all Syria was in his hands. Tahutmes III repeatedly raided Syria, bringing back plunder and captives year by year throughout most of his reign. The number of Syrian artists and of Syrian women brought into Egypt largely changed the style of art and the standard of beauty. Amenhotep III held all Syria in peace, and recorded his triumphs at the Euphrates on the walls of the temple of Soleb far up in Nubia. His monotheist son, Amenhotep IV, took the name of Akhenaton, “the glory of the sun's disc,” and established the worship of the radiant sun as the Aton, or Adon of Syria. The cuneiform letters from Tell el-Amarna place all this age before us in detail. There are some from the kings of the Amorites and Hittites, from Naharain and even Babylonia, to the great suzerain Amenhotep III. There is also the long series describing the gradual loss of Syria under Akhenaton, as written by the governors and chiefs, of the various towns. The main letters are summarized in the Students' History of Egypt, II, and full abstracts of all the letters are in Syria and Egypt, arranged in historical order.
Pal was reconquered by Seti I and his son Rameses II, but they only held about a third of the extent which formerly belonged to Amenhotep III. Merenptah, son of Rameses, also raided Southern Palestine. After that; it was left alone till the raid of Sheshenq in 933 bc. The only considerable assertion of Egyptian power was in Necoh's two raids up to the Euphrates, in 609 and 605 bc. But Egypt generally held the desert and a few minor points along the south border of Palestine. The Ptolemies seldom possessed more than that, their aspirations in Syria not lasting as permanent conquests. They were more successful in holding Cyprus.
2. Abramic Times
We now come to the specific connections of Egypt with the Old Testament. The movement of the family of Abram from Ur in the south of Mesopotamia up to Haran in the north (Gen_11:31) and thence down Syria into Egypt (Gen_12:5, Gen_12:10) was like that of the earlier Semitic “princes of the desert,” when they entered Egypt as the Hyksos kings about 2600 bc. Their earlier dominion was the 15th Dynasty of Egypt, and that was followed by another movement, the 16th Dynasty, about 2250 bc, which was the date of the migration of Terah from Ur. Thus the Abramic family took part in the second Hyksos movement. The cause of these tribal movements has been partly explained by Mr. Huntington's researches on the recurrence of dry periods in Asia (Royal Geogr. Soc., May 26, 1910: The Pulse of Asia). Such lack of rain forces the desert peoples on to the cultivated lands, and then later famines are recorded. The dry age which pushed the Arab tribes on to the Mediterranean in 640 ad was succeeded by famines in Egypt during 6 centuries So as soon as Abram moved into Syria a famine pushed him on to Egypt (Gen_12:10). To this succeeded other famines in Canaan (Gen_26:1), and later in both Canaan and Egypt (Gen_41:56; Gen_43:1; Gen_47:13). The migration of Abram was Thus conditioned by the general dry period, which forced the second Hyksos movement of which it was a part. The culture of the Hyksos was entirely nomadic, and agrees in all that we can trace with the patriarchal culture pictured in Gen.
3. Circumcision
Circumcision was a very ancient mutilation in Egypt, and is still kept up there by both Muslim and Christian. It was first adopted by Abram for Ishmael, the son of the Egyptian Hagar (Gen_16:3; Gen_17:23), before Isaac was promised. Hagar married Ishmael to an Egyptian (Gen_21:21), so that the Ishmaelites, or Hagarenes, of Gilead and Moab were three-quarters Egyptian.
At Gerar, in the south of Palestine, Egyptian was the prevailing race and language, as the general of Abimelech was Phichol, the Egyptian name Pa-khal, “the Syrian,” showing that the Gerarites were not Syrians.
4. Joseph
The history of Joseph rising to importance as a capable slave is perfectly natural in Egypt at that time, and equally so in later periods down to our own days. That this occurred during the Hyksos period is shown by the title given to Joseph - Abrekh, ('abhrēkh) (Gen_41:43) which is Abarakhu, the high Babylonian title. The names Zaphnath-paaneah, Asenath, and Potipherah have been variously equated in Egyptian, Naville seeing forms of the 18th Dynasty in them, but Spiegelberg, with more probability, seeing types of names of the 22nd Dynasty or later. The names are most likely an expansion of the original document; but there is not a single feature or incident in the relations of Joseph to the Egyptians which is at all improbable from the history and civilization that we know. See JOSEPH (1).
5. Descent into Egypt
The descent into Egypt and sojourn there are what might be expected of any Semitic tribe at this time. The allocation in Goshen (Gen_47:27) was the most suitable, as that was on the eastern border of the Delta, at the mouth of the Wady Tumilat, and was a district isolated from the general Egyptian population. The whole of Goshen is not more than 100 square miles, being bounded by the deserts, and by the large Egyptian city of Budastis on the West. The accounts of the embalming for 40 days and mourning for 70 days (Gen_50:3), and putting in a coffin (Gen_50:26) are exact. The 70 days' mourning existed both in the 1st Dynasty and in the 20th.
6. The Oppression
The oppression in Egypt began with a new king that knew not Joseph. This can hardly be other than the rise of the Berber conquerors who took the Delta from the Hyksos at the beginning of the 18th Dynasty, 1582 bc, and expelled the Hyksos into Syria. It could not be later than this, as the period of oppression in Egypt is stated at 4 centuries (Gen_15:13; Act_7:6), and the Exodus cannot be later than about 1220 bc, which leaves 360 years for the oppression. Also this length of oppression bars any much earlier date for the Exodus. The 360 years of oppression from 430 of the total sojourn in Egypt, leaves 70 years of freedom there. As Joseph died at 110 (
Gen_50:26), this implies that he was over 40 when his family came into Egypt, which would be quite consistent with the history.
7. The Historic Position
The store cities Pithom and Raamses are the sites Tell el-Maskhuta and Tell Rotāb in the Wady Tumilat, both built by Rameses II as frontier defenses. It is evident then that the serving with rigor was under that king, probably in the earlier part of his long reign of 67 years (1300-1234 bc), when he was actively campaigning in Palestine. This is shown in the narrative, for Moses was not yet born when the rigor began (Ex 1; Exo_2:2), and he grew up, slew an Egyptian, and then lived long in Midian before the king of Egypt died (Exo_2:23), perhaps 40 or 50 years after the rigorous servitude began, for he is represented as being 80 at the time of the Exodus (Deu_34:7). These numbers are probably not precise, but as a whole they agree well enough with Egyptian history. After the king died, Moses returned to Egypt, and began moving to get his kin away to the eastern deserts, with which he had been well acquainted in his exile from Egypt. A harsher servitude ensues, which might be expected from the more vigorous reign of Merenptah, after the slackness of the old age of Rameses. The campaign of Merenptah against Israel and other people in Palestine would not make him any less severe in his treatment of Semites in Egypt.
8. The Plagues
The plagues are in the order of usual seasonal troubles in Egypt, from the red unwholesome Nile in June, through the frogs, insects, hail and rain, locusts, and sandstorms in March. The death of the firstborn was in April at the Passover.
9. Date of the Exodus
The date of the Exodus is indicated as being about 1200 bc, by the 4 centuries of oppression, and by the names of the land and the city of Rameses (Gen_47:4; compare Exo_1:11). The historical limit is that the Egyptians were incessantly raiding Palestine down to 1194 bc, and then abandoned it till the invasion of Shishak. As there is no trace of these Egyptian invasions during all the ups and downs of the age of the Judges, it seems impossible to suppose the Israelites entered Canaan till after 1194 bc. The setting back of the Exodus much earlier has arisen from taking three simultaneous histories of the Judges as consecutive, as we shall notice farther on. The facts stated above, and the length of all three lines of the priestly genealogies, agree completely with the Egyptian history in putting the Exodus at about 1220 bc, and the entry into Canaan about 1180 bc.
10. Route of the Exodus
The route of the Exodus was first a concentration at Raamses or Tell Rotāb, in the Wady Tumliat, followed by a march to Succoth, a general name for the region of Bedawy booths; from there to Etham in the edge of the wilderness, about the modern Nefisheh. Thence they turned and encamped before Pi-hahiroth, the Egyptian Pa-qaheret, a Serapeum. Thus turning South to the West of the Red Sea (which then extended up to Tell el-Maskhuta), they had a Migdol tower behind them and Baal-zephon opposite to them. They were Thus “entangled in the land.” Then the strong east wind bared the shallows, and made it possible to cross the gulf and reach the opposite shore. They then went “Three days in the wilderness,” the three days' route without water to Marah, the bitter spring of Hawara, and immediately beyond reached Elim, which accords entirely with the Wady Gharandel. Thence they encamped by the Red Sea. All of this account exactly agrees with the traditional route down the West of the Sinaitic peninsula; it will not agree with any other route, and there is no reason to look for any different location of the march. See EXODUS, I.
11. Numbers of the Exodus
The numbers of the Israelites have long been a difficulty. On the one hand are the census lists (Nu 1; 2 and 26), with their summaries of 600,000 men besides children and a mixed multitude (Exo_12:37, Exo_12:38; Exo_38:26; Num_1:46; Num_11:21). On the other hand there are the exact statements of there being 22,273 firstborn, that is, fathers of families (Num_3:43), and that 40,000 armed men entered Canaan with Joshua (Jos_4:13), also the 35,000 who fought at Ai (Jos_8:3, Jos_8:12), and the 32,000 who fought against Midian (Jdg_7:3). Besides these, there are the general considerations that only 5,000 to 10,000 people could live in Goshen, that the Amalekites with whom the Israelites were equally matched (Exo_17:11) could not have exceeded about 5,000 in Sinai, that Moses judged all disputes, and that two midwives attended all the Israelite births, which would be 140 a day on a population of 600,000. Evidently, the statements of numbers are contradictory, and the external evidence is all in accord with lesser numbers. Proposals to reduce arbitrarily the larger numbers have been frequent; but there is one likely line of misunderstanding that may have originated the increase. In the census lists of the tribes, most of the hundreds in the numbers are 400 or 500, others are near those, and there are none whatever on 000, 100, 800 or 900. Evidently, the hundreds are independent of the thousands. Now in writing the statements, such as “Reuben, 46,500,” the original list would be 46 'eleph, 5 hundred people, and 'eleph means either “thousands” or else “groups” or “families.” Hence, a census of 46 tents, 500 people, would be ambiguous, and a later compiler might well take it as 46,500. In this way the whole census of 598 tents, 5,550 people, would be misread as 603,550 people. The checks on this are, that the number per tent should be reasonable in all cases, that the hundreds should not fluctuate more than the tents between the first and last census, and that the total should correspond to the known populations of Goshen and of Sinai; these requirements all agree with this reading of the lists. The ulterior details beyond the Egyptian period are dealt with in Egypt and Israel, 45, 55. See EXODUS, IV.
12. Israel in Canaan
Two points need notice here as incidentally bearing on the Egyptian connections: (1) The Israelites in Palestine before the Exodus, indicated by Merenptah triumphing over them there before 1230 bc, and the raids during the Egyptian residence (1Ch_7:21); (2) The triple history of the Judges, west, north, and east, each totaling to 120 years, in accord with the length of the four priestly genealogies (1Ch_6:4-8, 1Ch_6:22-28, 1Ch_6:33-35, 1Ch_6:39-43, 1Ch_6:44-47), and showing that the dates are about 1220 bc the Exodus, 1180 bc the entry to Canaan, 1150 bc the beginning of Judges, 1030 bc Saul (Egypt and Israel, 52-58).
13. Hadad
The connections with the monarchy soon begin. David and Joab attacked Edom (2Sa_8:14), and Hadad, the young king, was carried off by his servants to Egypt for safety. The Pharaoh who received and supported him must have been Siamen, the king of Zoan, which city was then an independent capital apart from the priest kings of Thebes (1Ki_11:15-22). Hadad was married to the Egyptian queen's sister when he grew up, probably in the reign of Pasebkhanu II.
14. Pharaoh's Daughter
The Pharaoh whose daughter was married to Solomon must have been the same Pasebkhanu; he reigned from 987-952 bc, and the marriage was about 970 in the middle of the reign. Another daughter of Pasebkhanu was Karamat, who was the wife of Shishak. Thus Solomon and Shishak married two sisters, and their aunt was queen of Edom. This throws light on the politics of the kingdoms. Probably Solomon had some child by Pharaoh's daughter, and the Egyptians would expect that to be the heir. Shishak's invasion, on the death of Solomon, was perhaps based upon the right of a nephew to the throne of Judah.
15. Shishak
The invasion of Shishak (Egyptian, Sheshenq) took place probably at the end of his reign. His troops were Lubim (Libyans), Sukkim (men of Succoth, the east border) and Kushim (Ethiopians). The account of the war is on the side of the great fore-court at Karnak, which shows long lists of places in Judah, agreeing with the subjugation recorded in 1Ki_14:25, 1Ki_14:26, and 2Ch_12:2-4.
16. Zerakh
Zerakh, or Usarkon, was the next king of Egypt, the son of Karamat, Solomon's sister-in-law. He invaded Judah unsuccessfully in 903 bc (2Ch_14:9) with an army of Libyans and Sudanis (2Ch_16:8). A statue of the Nile, dedicated by him, and naming his descent from Karamat and Pasebkhanu, is in the British Museum.
17. The Ethiopians
After a couple of centuries the Ethiopian kings intervened. Shabaka was appointed viceroy of Egypt by his father Piankhy, and is described by the Assyrians as Sibe, commander-in-chief of Muzri, and by the Hebrews as Sua or So, king of Egypt (2Ki_17:4). Tirhakah next appears as a viceroy, and Hezekiah was warned against trusting to him (2Ki_19:9). These two kings touch on Jewish history during their vice-royalties, before their full reigns began. Necoh next touches on Judah in his raid to Carchemish in 609 bc, when he slew Josiah for opposing him (2Ki_23:29, 2Ki_23:30; 2Ch_35:20-24).
18. Tahpanhes
After the taking of Jerusalem, for fear of vengeance for the insurrection of Ishmael (2Ki_25:25, 2Ki_25:26; Jer 40; 41; 42), the remnant of the Jews fled to the frontier fortress of Egypt, Tahpanhes, Tehaphnehes, Greek Daphnae, modern Defenneh, about 10 miles West of the present Suez Canal (Jer_43:7-13). The brick pavement in front of the entrance to the fortress there, in which Jeremiah hid the stones, has been uncovered and the fortress completely planned. It was occupied by Greeks, who there brought Greek words and things into contact with the traveling Jews for a couple of generations before the fall of Jerusalem.
19. Hophra
The prophecy that Hophra would be delivered to them that sought his life (Jer_44:30) was fulfilled, as he was kept captive by his successor, Amasis, for 3 years, and after a brief attempt at liberty, he was strangled.
20. The Jews at Syene
The account of the Jews settled in Egypt (Jer 44) is singularly illustrated by the Aramaic Jewish papyri found at Syene (Aswan). These show the use of Aramaic and of oaths by Yahu, as stated of 5 cities in Egypt (
Isa_19:18). The colony at Syene was well-to-do, though not rich; they were householders who possessed all their property by regular title-deeds, who executed marriage settlements, and were fully used to litigation, having in deeds of sale a clause that no other deed could be valid. The temple of Yahu filled the space between two roads, and faced upon 3 houses, implying a building about 60 or 70 ft. wide. It was built of hewn stone, with stone columns, 7 gates, and a cedar roof. It was destroyed in 410, after lasting from before Cambyses in 525 bc, and a petition for rebuilding it was granted in 407.
21. The New Jerusalem of Oniah
The most flourishing period of the Jews in Egypt was when Oniah IV, the son of the rightful high priest Oniah, was driven from Jerusalem by the abolition of Jewish worship and ordinances under Antiochus. In 170 bc he fled to Egypt, and there established a new Jerusalem with a temple and sacrifices as being the only way to maintain the Jewish worship. Oniah IV was a valiant man, general to queen Cleopatra I; and he offered to form the Jewish community into a frontier guard on the East of Egypt, hating the Syrians to the uttermost, if the Jews might form their own community. They so dominated the eastern Delta that troops of Caesar could not pass from Syria to Alexandria without their assent. The new Jerusalem was 20 miles North of Cairo, a site now known as Tell el-Yehudiyeh. The great mound of the temple still remains there, with the Passover ovens beneath it, and part of the massive stone fortifications on the front of it. This remained a stronghold of free Judaism until after Titus took Jerusalem; and it was only when the Zealots tried to make it a center of insurrection, that at last it was closed and fell into decay. Josephus is the original authority for this history (see Egypt and Israel, 97-110).
22. The Egyptian Jew
The Jew in Egypt followed a very different development from the Babylonian Jew, and this Egyptian type largely influenced Christianity. In the colony at Syene a woman named “Trust Yahweh” had no objection to swearing by the Egyptian goddess Seti when making an Egyptian contract; and in Jer_44:15-19, the Jews boasted of their heathen worship in Egypt. Oniah had no scruple in establishing a temple and sacrifices apart from Jerusalem, without any of the particularism of the Maccabean zealots. Philo at Alexandria labored all his life for the union of Jewish thought with Greek philosophy. The Hermetic books show how, from 500 to 200 bc, religious thought was developing under eclectic influence of Egyptian Jewish, Persian, Indian and Greek beliefs, and producing the tenets about the second God, the Eternal Son, who was the Logos, and the types of Conversion, as the Divine Ray, the New Birth, and the Baptism. Later the Wisdom literature of Alexandria, 200-100 bc, provided the basis of thought and simile on which the Pauline Epistles were built. The great wrench in the history of the church came when it escaped from the Babylonian-Jewish formalism of the Captivity, which ruled at Jerusalem, and grew into the wider range of ideas of the Alexandrian Jews. These ideas had been preserved in Egypt from the days of the monarchy, and had developed a great body of religious thought and phraseology from their eclectic connections. The relations of Christianity with Egypt are outside our scope, but some of them will be found in Egypt and Israel, 124-41.
23. Cities and Places Alphabetically
The Egyptian cities, places and peoples named in the Old Testament may briefly be noted. AVEN (Ezk_30:17) or ON (Gen_41:45) is the 'An of Egyptian, the Greek Heliopolis, now Matarieh, 7 miles North of Cairo. It was the seat of prehistoric government, the royal emblems were kept there as the sacred relics of the temple, and its high priest was “the great seer,” one of the greatest of the religious officials. The schools of Heliopolis were celebrated, and it seems to have always been a center of learning. The site is now marked by the great enclosure of the temple, and one obelisk of Senusert (12th Dynasty). It was here that the Egyptian kings had at their installation to come and bathe in the lake in which the sun bathes daily, the 'Ainesh-Shems, or “Lake of the Sun” of the Arabs, connected with the fresh spring here which Christian tradition attributes to the visit of the Virgin and Child. The great sycamore tree here is the successor of that under which the Virgin is said to have rested.
BAAL-ZEPHON was a shrine on the eastern site of the head of the Red Sea, a few miles South of Ismailiyeh; no trace is now known of it (Exo_14:2).
CUSHIM or Ethiopians were a part of the Egyptian army of Shishak and of Usarkon (2Ch_12:3; 2Ch_16:8). The army was in 4 brigades, that of Ptah of Memphis, central Egypt; that of Amen of Thebes, Southern Egypt and Ethiopia; that of Set of the eastern frontier (Sukkim); and that of Ra, Heliopolis and the Delta.
GOSHEN was a fertile district at the west end of the Wady Tumilat, 40 to 50 miles Northeast of Cairo. It was bounded by the deserts on the North and Southeast, and by the Egyptian city of Bubastis on the West. Its area was not over 100 square miles; it formerly supported 4,000 Bedouin and now about 12,000 cultivators.
LUBIM, the Libyans who formed part of the Egyptian army as light-armed archers, from very early times.
MIGDOL is the name of any tower, familiar also as Magdala. It was applied to some watchtower on the West of the Red Sea, probably on the high land above the Serapeum.
No is Thebes, in Assyrian Nia, from the Egyptian Nu, “the city.” This was the capital of the 12th Dynasty, and of the 17th-21st Dynasties. Owing to the buildings being of sandstone, which is not of much use for reworking, they have largely remained since the desolation of the city under Ptolemy X. The principal divisions of the site are: (1) Karnak, with the temple of the 12th Dynasty, built over by all the successive kings of the 18th Dynasty, and enlarged by Seti I and Rameses II, and by Shishak, Tirhakah, and the Ptolemies. The whole temple of Amon and its subsidiary temples form the largest mass of ruins that is known. (2) Luqsor, the temple to commemorate the divine birth of Amenhotep III (1440 bc), added to by Rameses II. (3) The funerary temples, bordering the western shore, of the kings of the 18th to 20th Dynasties. These have mostly been destroyed, by the unscrupulous quarrying done by each king on the work of his predecessors; the only temple in fair condition is that of Rameses III, which is left because no later king required its material for building. (4) The great cemetery, ranging from the splendid rock halls of the Tombs of the Kings, covered with paintings, down to the humblest graves. For any detailed account see either Baedeker's or Murray's Guides, or Weigall's Guide to Antiquities.
NOPH, the Egyptian Men-nofer, Greek Memphis, now Mitraheny, 12 miles South of Cairo. This was the capital from the foundation at the beginning of the dynasties. Thebes and Alexandria shared its importance, but it was the seat of government down to the Arab invasion. In Roman times it was as large as London North of the Thames. The outlying parts are now all buried by the rise of the soil, but more than a mile length of ruins yet remains, which are now being regularly worked over by the British School. The heart of the city is the great metropolitan temple of Ptah, nearly all of which is now under 10 feet of soil, and under water most of the year. This is being excavated in sections, as it is all private property. At the north end of the ruins is the palace mound, on which has been cleared the palace of Apries (Hophra). Other temples have been located, as well as the foreign quarter containing early Greek pottery and the temple of Proteus named by Herodotus (see Memphis, I, II, III).
PATHROS is the usual name for Upper Egypt in the prophets. It is the Egyptian Pa-ta-res, “the south land.”
PI-BESETH is the Egyptian Pa-Bast, Greek Bubastis, at the eastern side of the Delta, the city of the cat-headed goddess Bast. The ruins are still large, and the temple site has been excavated, producing sculptures from the 4th Dynasty onward.
PITHOM is the Egyptian Pa-Tum, the city of the Sun-god Tum or Atmu, who was worshipped on the East of the Delta. The site has remains of the fortress of Rameses II, built by the Israelites, and is now known as Tell el-Maskhuta, 11 miles West of Ismailia.
RAAMSES is the other city built by the Israelites, now Tell Rotāb, 20 miles West of Ismailia. A wailed camp existed here from early times, and the temple of Rameses was built on the top of the older ruins. A large part of the temple front is now at Philadelphia, excavated by the British School.

Paul was a man who knew prison cells, beatings, hunger, and the threat of death, and he died still preaching what he believed. He listed his own record, more imprisonments, countless stripes, five times thirty nine lashes from the Jews, three beatings with rods, one stoning, three shipwrecks, nights without sleep, cold, and nakedness. After his arrest in Jerusalem he sat two years in Caesarea, then two more years under guard in Rome, and from those bonds he kept teaching Christ with all boldness. Near the end he wrote that he was already being poured out, that the time of his departure had come, that he had fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. Church memory places his death in Rome under Nero, by the sword, between the years 64 and 67.

It is like I told my pastor, you can discredit what cannot be proved, but most people look right past what can be proved.

The church did not start with power, money, or an army. After Jesus was taken up, about one hundred twenty believers waited in Jerusalem. On the day of Pentecost Peter stood and said God had raised Jesus, whom they had crucified, and about three thousand received the word and were baptized. Soon the number of the men who believed was about five thousand, and the word of God continued to increase, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. When the rulers in Jerusalem saw the boldness of Peter and John, they perceived that they were uneducated and common men, and they marveled, because they recognized that they had been with Jesus. Paul later wrote the same truth about the whole movement, not many were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth, but God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and what is weak in the world to shame the strong.

They had nothing to offer but the word of a crucified and risen Messiah. To Jews that word was a stumbling block, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree. To Greeks it was foolishness. They carried that word in one of the most dangerous hours of the ancient world, first under leaders who stoned Stephen and killed James the brother of John, then under Rome, when Nero blamed Christians for the fire of 64 and made a public spectacle of their deaths. The persecution that was meant to end them scattered the believers from Jerusalem, and those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Within a generation the message had reached Judea, Samaria, Syria, Asia Minor, Greece, and the city of Rome itself.

What can be measured is the mismatch. A handful of fishermen, a tax collector, and a former persecutor of the church, with no swords and no offices, spoke to people who had every reason to silence them. By the close of the first century, careful estimates still put the whole church in the low thousands in an empire of tens of millions. By the year 300, before any emperor favored the faith, those same kinds of estimates place Christians in the millions, a large and growing share of the Roman world. Many who heard were willing to lose property, status, and life rather than deny what they had received.

That is why this can be seen as a true miracle. Ordinary calculation struggles to explain why a message this costly, preached by men this weak, in a climate this hostile, took root and spread. Acts says the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. Paul said the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. You can argue about what cannot be placed under a lamp in a laboratory. What can be proved is the small beginning, the public preaching, the chains, the hatred, and the growth that followed anyway. Most people look right past those facts while they debate the rest.

text:
Dinesh D’Souza @DineshDSouza offers apologetic explanations for both Paul’s “revelation” and Pharaoh’s stubbornness—because the biblical accounts themselves create serious problems.

None of it is established fact.

Paul could have invented the story of his revelation on the road to Damascus. His claim that the resurrected Jesus appeared to him became enormously self-serving: it gave him authority and influence in the emerging Christian movement. He even claimed that Jesus appeared to more than 500 people at once. Yet not one is named, and apparently not one left a record of this extraordinary event.

Then there is Pharaoh.

After roughly 400 years in Egypt, much of it supposedly spent in slavery—a claim for which there is no archaeological evidence—God decides it is time to free His “chosen people.” Moses and Aaron deliver the ultimatum. Plague after plague follows. Pharaoh repeatedly relents, or God hardens Pharaoh’s heart and changes the outcome.

The contradiction is obvious: if God wanted the Israelites freed, why not simply change Pharaoh’s mind immediately? No negotiations. No plagues. No mass suffering. No need to override Pharaoh’s will.

Instead, God repeatedly interferes with Pharaoh’s decisions—and finally with the natural order itself by parting the Red Sea, allowing the Israelites to escape while the pursuing Egyptian army drowns.

All this, we are told, was necessary so God could demonstrate His power.

But if God can intervene in human will and suspend the laws of nature when He chooses, the free-will defense becomes deeply problematic.

Why part the Red Sea but not open the gates of the Nazi death camps?

Why intervene to defeat Pharaoh’s army but allow the 9/11 hijackers to complete their mission?

The problem is not merely explaining why God permits evil. It is the apparently arbitrary way in which this supposedly omnipotent God chooses when to override human free will and the natural order—while leaving countless innocent believers to suffer.

Is God perhaps unable to balance between the free will of the perpetrators and the free will of the many victims?

Apologetics can provide (often far-fetched)“explanations”. It cannot turn contradictions into evidence.

text:
Does Israel have a right to exist?

What did Albert Einstein think? He fled the Nazis. He lost colleagues to the Holocaust. He was offered the presidency of Israel, and turned it down.

Albert Einstein's answer:

"I should much rather see reasonable agreement with the Arabs on the basis of living together in peace than the creation of a Jewish state.

text:
Today is the feast of St. Hermione the daughter of Philip the Evangelist. Hermione went from her father's house in Caesarea to Ephesus to look for the Apostle John. When she arrived, she was told that John was gone. Hermione was disappointed but she found others imitating the Apostles such as Petronius, a disciple of Paul. Hermione was a trained doctor who could also heal with miracles. She never charged money to heal anyone, so people came no matter how poor they were.

When the Emperor Trajan went to war with the Persians, he ordered all the Empire to offer sacrifices to the gods. He knew that Hermione was the reason no one would sacrifice to false gods in Ephesus, so he had Hermione publicly beaten. She remained resolute, and Tajan was so impressed with her Faith that for all his reign he allowed Ephesians to keep worshipping Jesus. This lasted until Hadrian came to rule.

Hadrian cast Hermione into a boiling cauldron, burning his hand, but Hermione emerged unharmed. Then Hermione said to the Emperor "I have a great sacrifice to do to Hercules. You have served him little, but I will serve him much". So Hadrian led her to the Hercules' Temple, but she commanded the idols to shatter into millions of pieces. Hadrian ordered two guards named Theodoulos and Timothy to seize Hermione but their hands shrivelled. She healed them and they were baptised so Hadrian let her go and she died in peace decades later.

Merciful God, whose most dear Son came to heal the sick, raise the dead, cast out demons, and preach good news to the poor: Lead us by the example of your servant Hermione, to freely give even as we have freely received; through Jesus Christ our Lord. ᴀᴍᴇɴ.

text:
Jesus Calling: September 4th  
In closeness to Me, you are safe. In the intimacy of My Presence, you are energized. No matter where you are in the world, you know you belong when you sense My nearness. Ever since the Fall, man has experienced a gaping emptiness that only My Presence can fill. I designed you for close communication with your Creator. How I enjoyed walking in the garden with Adam and Eve, before the evil one deceived them!  
     When you commune with Me in the garden of your heart, both you and I are blessed. This is My way of living in the world--through you! Together we will push back the darkness, for I am the Light of the World.  
  
RELATED BIBLE VERSES:  
  
Psalm 32:7 (NLT)  
7 For you are my hiding place;  
    you protect me from trouble.  
    You surround me with songs of victory.  
  
Genesis 3:8-9 (NLT)  
8 When the cool evening breezes were blowing, the man and his wife heard the Lord God walking about in the garden. So they hid from the Lord God among the trees. 9 Then the Lord God called to the man, “Where are you?”  
  
Additional insight regarding Genesis 3:7,8: After sinning, Adam and Eve felt guilt and embarrassment over their nakedness. Their guilty feeling made them try to hide from God. A guilty conscience is a warning signal God placed inside you that goes off when you've done wrong. The worst step you can take is to eliminate the guilty feelings without eliminating the cause. That would be like using a painkiller but not treating the disease. Be glad those guilty feelings are there. They make you aware of your sin so you can ask God's forgiveness and then correct your wrongdoing.  
  
Additional insight regarding Genesis 3:8: The thought of two humans covered with fig leaves trying to hide from the all-seeing, all-knowing God is humorous. How could they be so silly as to think they could actually hide? Yet we do the same, acting as though God doesn't know what we're doing. Have the courage to share all you do and think with him. And don't try to hide - it can't be done. Honesty will strengthen your relationship.  
  
Additional insight regarding Genesis 3:8,9: These verses show God's desire to have fellowship with us. They also show why we are afraid to have fellowship with him. Adam and Eve hid from God when they heard him approaching. God wanted to be with them, but because of their sin, they were afraid to show themselves. Sin had broken their close relationship with God, just as it has broken ours. But Jesus Christ, God's Son, opens the way for us to renew our fellowship with him. God longs to be with us. He actively offers us his unconditional love. Our natural response is fear because we feel we can't live up to his standards. But understanding that he loves us, regardless of our faults, can help remove the dread.  
  
John 8:12 (NLT)  
Jesus, the Light of the World  
12 Jesus spoke to the people once more and said, “I am the light of the world. If you follow me, you won’t have to walk in darkness, because you will have the light that leads to life.”  
  
Additional insight regarding John 8:12: Jesus was speaking in the Treasury - the part of the Temple where the offerings were put (John 8:20) and where candles burned to symbolize the pillar of fire that led the people of Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22). In this context, Jesus called himself the light of the world. The pillar of fire represented God's presence, protection, and guidance. Likewise, Jesus brings God's presence, protection, and guidance. Is Jesus the light of your world?  
  
Additional insight regarding John 8:12 from John 1:4-5 - "The World gave life to everything that was created, and his life brought light to everyone. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness can never extinguish it.": "The darkness can never extinguish it" means the darkness of evil never has and never will overcome God's light. Jesus Christ is the Creator of life, and his life brings light to humankind. In his light, we see ourselves as we really are (sinners in need of a Savior). https://t.co/ainHLl0QUu

text:
The rapture error continues to persist even in the face of sound doctrine of the written Word. I dismantle each of the 29 claims for a secret "rapture" and show that the Bible clearly tells us God's people are sealed and protected through the tribulation not extracted. 

Claim 1 - The Church is explicitly told that God “hath not appointed us to wrath.” 1 Thessalonians 5:9

Granted, and it stands. The Bride is not appointed to wrath. Scripture names where wrath is: "the seven last plagues, for in them is filled up the wrath of God" (Revelation 15:1). Trumpets are warning judgments that call the world to repent (Revelation 9:20-21); bowls are wrath. She is gathered at the last trumpet and is not present for the bowls. The promise is kept without a secret exit.

Claim 2 - Jesus is the One “which delivered us from the wrath to come.” 1 Thessalonians 1:10

Same answer, and note what the verse says He delivers from: "the wrath to come." It does not say "the tribulation to come." Substituting one for the other is the whole argument, assumed rather than proved.

Claim 3 - The Church is promised deliverance from “the hour of temptation” coming upon the whole world, not merely protection during part of it. Revelation 3:10

Revelation 3:10 is the strongest verse on the list and it cuts the other way. The construction is tēreō ek, keep from. Messiah uses that exact construction in John 17:15: "I pray not that Thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that Thou shouldest keep them from the evil." Kept from, explicitly while left in. That is the Passover pattern: Israel was not evacuated from Egypt before the plagues, she was marked with blood on the doorpost and preserved through them.

Claim 4 - The rapture passage ends with comfort: “Wherefore comfort one another with these words.” A doctrine placing the Bride deep inside Daniel’s seventieth week turns comfort into survival planning. 1 Thessalonians 4:18

Read verse 13 for the occasion. The Thessalonians were grieving over believers who had died. The comfort Paul gives is the resurrection: your dead are not lost, they rise first. The comfort is that death does not win, not that the Bride avoids hardship. Every martyr under the altar in Revelation 6:9 was comforted by that same promise and was not extracted.

Claim 5 - The Church is told to wait for God’s Son from Heaven, not to wait for Antichrist, the mark, the abomination, or the midpoint. 1 Thessalonians 1:10

Granted, we wait for the Son. Paul himself sequences it in 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3, and he opens by naming the very subject: "our gathering together unto Him." Then he says that day will not come "except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed." Paul puts two events in front of the gathering. The list never touches this passage.

Claim 6 - Our heavenly expectation is the Saviour Himself: “from whence also we look for the Saviour.” Philippians 3:20

True and unchallenged. Philippians 3:20 states the object of hope, not its timing. No verse on the list yet supplies the timing.

Claim 7 - Titus calls Christ’s appearing “that blessed hope,” not the blessed opportunity to identify the Beast before escaping him. Titus 2:13

Titus 2:13 calls it "the glorious appearing," epiphaneia. Paul uses the same word in 2 Thessalonians 2:8 for the appearing that destroys the lawless one. One appearing, one word, and it is anything but secret.

Claim 8 - The Lord Himself descends for the Church with a shout, the voice of the archangel, and the trump of God. 1 Thessalonians 4:16

This is an argument against the position it is offered to support. A shout, an archangel's voice, and the trump of God is the loudest event in the Canon. And 1 Corinthians 15:52 identifies which trumpet: the last one.

Claim 9 - The dead in Christ rise first at the rapture. That resurrection is part of the Church’s own program. 1 Thessalonians 4:16

Granted. Revelation 20:4-6 calls that rising "the first resurrection," and places it after the beast and his image. At the seventh trumpet the announcement is "the time of the dead, that they should be judged" (Revelation 11:18). The resurrection is dated in the text, and it is not before the trumpets.

Claim 10 - Living Church-Age saints are caught up together with the resurrected saints to meet Christ “in the air.” 1 Thessalonians 4:17

Granted, and the word is together. One gathering, one Bride. To make this work as a pre-tribulation event you need a second gathering later for a second set of saints, which the Canon never mentions. The Bride is one body: believing Judah, Israel in exile, and the sojourner grafted in (Ephesians 2:11-22).

Claim 11 - The rapture takes believers upward to meet Christ; the Second Advent brings Christ and His saints downward to earth. 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 19:11-14

Apantēsis, the word for "meet," is the civic reception. The citizens go out to meet the arriving king and escort him back in. It is used that way in Acts 28:15 when the brethren come out to meet Paul on the Appian Way, and in Matthew 25:6 when the virgins go out to meet the Bridegroom. They do not go out and stay out. Meeting the descending King in the air is the reception party, not a round trip with a seven year layover.

Claim 12 - Revelation 19 shows saints already in Heaven and returning with Christ. They had to go up before they could come back down. Revelation 19:14

Granted that they are in heaven, and no gap is required to get them there. They were gathered at the seventh trumpet in Revelation 11:15, which precedes the bowls and precedes chapter 19 by the book's own inviolable sequence: seals, then trumpets, then bowls.

Claim 13 - The armies returning with Christ are clothed in “fine linen, white and clean,” connecting them with the redeemed company already in Heaven. Revelation 19:8, 14

Granted. Revelation 19:8 defines the linen as "the righteousness of saints." The armies also include the heavenly host (Matthew 25:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7). This proves the saints return with Him. It says nothing about when they went up.

Claim 14 - Daniel’s seventieth week concerns “thy people” and “thy holy city” - Daniel’s people are Israel and the city is Jerusalem. Daniel 9:24

This is where the position pays its heaviest price. Read the purposes the seventy sevens were decreed to accomplish (Daniel 9:24): to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, to anoint the Most Holy. If the seventieth week is still future, then sin has not been ended and reconciliation has not been made. Those six were finished at the Cross and at Pentecost. The decree is closed.

Claim 15 - Daniel 9 never identifies the Body of Christ as the subject of the seventieth week. Daniel 9:24-27

Correct, and Daniel 9 never identifies Antichrist as the subject either. The nearest antecedent of the "he" in verse 27 is Messiah the Prince from verses 25-26. And the one who "shall confirm the covenant with many" is the One who said over the cup, "this is My blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28). That is Daniel 9:27 quoted at the Table.

Claim 16 - The seventieth week resumes Israel’s prophetic clock; the Church is a mystery revealed through Paul. Romans 11:25; Ephesians 3:1-9

The gap is supplied, not stated. Daniel gives seven sevens, then sixty-two sevens, then Messiah cut off, then one seven. There is no text placing two thousand years between week sixty-nine and week seventy. A doctrine that requires an unstated interval longer than the entire prophecy has to argue for that interval, and the list does not.

Claim 17 - Paul calls the Body of Christ a “mystery” that was not made known in other ages as it is now revealed. Ephesians 3:3-6

Read the definition Paul gives of the mystery in the very next verses: "that the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body" (Ephesians 3:6). The mystery is not that God started a second people. It is that the two became one. Ephesians 2:14-16: He broke down the middle wall and made "one new man." The chapter cited to establish two programs is the chapter that abolishes them.

Claim 18 - Israel’s temporary blindness lasts “until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.” Romans 11:25

Granted. Blindness in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles. Nothing here concerns the timing of a gathering.

Claim 19 - After the Gentile fullness, God turns prophetically again toward Israel. Romans 11:25-27

And He turns to them by the picture Paul actually draws: one olive tree. Natural branches broken off through unbelief, wild branches grafted in, natural branches grafted back into the same tree (Romans 11:17-24). Not two trees, not two programs, not two Brides. Romans 11 is the end of the two-people system, not its charter.

Claim 20 - Jeremiah calls the coming unparalleled trouble “the time of Jacob’s trouble,” not the time of the Church’s trouble. Jeremiah 30:7

Finish the verse. "It is even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he shall be saved out of it" (Jeremiah 30:7). Saved out of, from inside. Noah in the ark, Israel in Goshen, blood on the doorpost, the three in the furnace. The covenant pattern is preservation through, never extraction before.

Claim 21 - Matthew 24’s setting is explicitly Jewish: Judaea is named. Matthew 24:16

Granted, and the setting is even more specific than that. The disciples asked about the stones of the temple (Matthew 24:2-3). Judaea, the housetop, the winter flight, and the desolation all landed in AD 70, which is exactly why Messiah could say "this generation shall not pass" (24:34).

Claim 22 - Matthew 24 tells people to pray that their flight be not on the sabbath day - language belonging naturally to Israel’s prophetic setting. Matthew 24:20

Granted, and it points the same direction. Sabbath-day flight is a first-century Judean concern, which supports the AD 70 fulfillment, not a future seven-year program.

Claim 23 - Matthew 24 refers directly to Daniel’s “abomination of desolation.” Matthew 24:15; Daniel 9:27

It does, and Daniel 9:27 finds its end in the Cross, where sacrifice and offering ceased in truth and the veil tore from the top down (Matthew 27:51). AD 70 then removed the shadow's remaining machinery. The type is real, and a greater fulfillment remains.

Claim 24 - The temple is therefore part of Israel’s Tribulation program, not a sign the Church is commanded to await before the rapture. Matthew 24:15

Here is the problem with quarantining Matthew 24. That same chapter contains the watch-and-be-ready charge, "he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved" (24:13), and the parables of the servants. Pre-tribulation preaching uses those constantly. You cannot assign the chapter to Israel and preach it to the Bride on Sunday. And 24:31 has a great trumpet and a gathering of the elect, placed by verse 29 after the tribulation of those days.

Claim 25 - Christ never tells the Body of Christ to monitor temple construction as the prerequisite to our blessed hope.

Fully granted, and the covenant goes further than the objection. There is no third temple in the program at all. Messiah's risen body is the Temple (John 2:19-21), and by the Holy Spirit the Bride is the Temple (1 Corinthians 3:16, 6:19). Watching Jerusalem for cornerstone announcements is watching for the return of a shadow that the Resurrection retired.

Claim 26 - The Church’s rapture doctrine is given through Paul, while Matthew 24 describes the Tribulation and visible Second Advent. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18; Matthew 24:15-31

Paul states his source in 1 Thessalonians 4:15: "this we say unto you by the word of the Lord." He is handing on the Lord's teaching, not launching a separate program. And when he takes the subject up again in 2 Thessalonians 2, he front-loads it with the falling away and the revealing of the man of sin.

Claim 27 - Matthew 24’s gathering follows cosmic signs and the visible appearing of the Son of man; 1 Thessalonians 4 describes the Church meeting Christ in the air. Matthew 24:29-31; 1 Thessalonians 4:17

Lay the four texts side by side. Matthew 24:29-31: cosmic signs, then a great trumpet, then the gathering of the elect. 1 Corinthians 15:52: the last trumpet, then the change. 1 Thessalonians 4:16: the trump of God, then the gathering. Revelation 11:15-18: the seventh trumpet, the Kingdom proclaimed, the time of the dead. One trumpet, four witnesses, one event.

Claim 28 - The rapture is described as a mystery: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” 1 Corinthians 15:51

The mystery is named in the clause itself: not everyone will die. That is the surprise, not secrecy. And Paul dates it in the very next breath.

Claim 29 - That change happens “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” 1 Corinthians 15:52

Which brings the list to its own undoing. Verse 52 in full: "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump." The list quotes the speed and stops at the comma. Speed is not secrecy, and the timing stamp was in the verse the whole time.

All twenty-nine reasons reduce to three assumptions, and none of the three is stated in the text. 

The first is that wrath means the entire seven years rather than the bowls, though Revelation 15:1 says the wrath of God is filled up in the seven last plagues, and the trumpets before them are warnings that call the world to repent. 

The second is that Daniel's seventieth week is future and empty, though the six things the seventy sevens were decreed to accomplish (Daniel 9:24) include making an end of sins and reconciliation for iniquity, which means a future seventieth week leaves the Cross unfinished. 

The third is that there are two peoples running two programs, though Ephesians 2 says the wall came down and the two became one new man, and Romans 11 draws one olive tree with branches broken off and grafted back into the same root. 

Strip those three and the list has no timing argument left, only true statements about our hope that say nothing about when.

Conclusion

The timing was never hidden. 

It sits in the same verses the list quotes, one clause past where the quotation stops. "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump" (1 Corinthians 15:52). 

The last trumpet is the seventh, and when it sounds the Kingdom is proclaimed and the time of the dead has come (Revelation 11:15-18). 

Messiah prayed plainly, "I pray not that Thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that Thou shouldest keep them from the evil" (John 17:15). 

That is the whole pattern of the Word: 
Noah shut in the ark, Israel behind blood on the doorpost while the destroyer passed over, Goshen untouched while Egypt fell, the three men in the furnace with a fourth beside them. 

Every time, preserved through it, never lifted out of it before it started. 

The Bride is sealed before the trumpets fall (Revelation 7:3), kept through them, and gathered at the last one. 

She is not appointed to wrath and she will not see the bowls. 

That promise is kept in full without inventing a secret coming the Canon never describes, and a doctrine that has to stop reading in the middle of a verse to survive is not resting on the written Word.

🚨‼️50 Reasons I Am Pre-Trib and Not Pre-Wrath🚨‼️

1 - The Church is explicitly told that God “hath not appointed us to wrath.” 1 Thessalonians 5:9

2 - Jesus is the One “which delivered us from the wrath to come.” 1 Thessalonians 1:10

3 - The Church is promised deliverance from “the hour of temptation” coming upon the whole world, not merely protection during part of it. Revelation 3:10

4 - The rapture passage ends with comfort: “Wherefore comfort one another with these words.” A doctrine placing the Bride deep inside Daniel’s seventieth week turns comfort into survival planning. 1 Thessalonians 4:18

5 - The Church is told to wait for God’s Son from Heaven, not to wait for Antichrist, the mark, the abomination, or the midpoint. 1 Thessalonians 1:10

6 - Our heavenly expectation is the Saviour Himself: “from whence also we look for the Saviour.” Philippians 3:20

7 - Titus calls Christ’s appearing “that blessed hope,” not the blessed opportunity to identify the Beast before escaping him. Titus 2:13

8 - The Lord Himself descends for the Church with a shout, the voice of the archangel, and the trump of God. 1 Thessalonians 4:16

9 - The dead in Christ rise first at the rapture. That resurrection is part of the Church’s own program. 1 Thessalonians 4:16

10 - Living Church-Age saints are caught up together with the resurrected saints to meet Christ “in the air.” 1 Thessalonians 4:17

11 - The rapture takes believers upward to meet Christ; the Second Advent brings Christ and His saints downward to earth. 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 19:11-14

12 - Revelation 19 shows saints already in Heaven and returning with Christ. They had to go up before they could come back down. Revelation 19:14

13 - The armies returning with Christ are clothed in “fine linen, white and clean,” connecting them with the redeemed company already in Heaven. Revelation 19:8, 14

14 - Daniel’s seventieth week concerns “thy people” and “thy holy city” - Daniel’s people are Israel and the city is Jerusalem. Daniel 9:24

15 - Daniel 9 never identifies the Body of Christ as the subject of the seventieth week. Daniel 9:24-27

16 - The seventieth week resumes Israel’s prophetic clock; the Church is a mystery revealed through Paul. Romans 11:25; Ephesians 3:1-9

17 - Paul calls the Body of Christ a “mystery” that was not made known in other ages as it is now revealed. Ephesians 3:3-6

18 - Israel’s temporary blindness lasts “until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.” Romans 11:25

19 - After the Gentile fullness, God turns prophetically again toward Israel. Romans 11:25-27

20 - Jeremiah calls the coming unparalleled trouble “the time of Jacob’s trouble,” not the time of the Church’s trouble. Jeremiah 30:7

21 - Matthew 24’s setting is explicitly Jewish: Judaea is named. Matthew 24:16

22 - Matthew 24 tells people to pray that their flight be not on the sabbath day - language belonging naturally to Israel’s prophetic setting. Matthew 24:20

23 - Matthew 24 refers directly to Daniel’s “abomination of desolation.” Matthew 24:15; Daniel 9:27

24 - The temple is therefore part of Israel’s Tribulation program, not a sign the Church is commanded to await before the rapture. Matthew 24:15

25 - Christ never tells the Body of Christ to monitor temple construction as the prerequisite to our blessed hope.

26 - The Church’s rapture doctrine is given through Paul, while Matthew 24 describes the Tribulation and visible Second Advent. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18; Matthew 24:15-31

27 - Matthew 24’s gathering follows cosmic signs and the visible appearing of the Son of man; 1 Thessalonians 4 describes the Church meeting Christ in the air. Matthew 24:29-31; 1 Thessalonians 4:17

28 - The rapture is described as a mystery: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” 1 Corinthians 15:51

29 - That change happens “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” 1 Corinthians 15:52

You hopped in and struck a thesis the post did not hold. No one claimed ordinary mission from a living pope. The claim is indefectibility: the Church cannot lose the means Christ instituted. 

After multiple successions of heretical illegitimate occupiers who attacked the papacy itself, that means supplied jurisdiction is offered by the Church and that the remedy is a council of Catholic bishops.

It is not the Western Schism, a crisis that had several claimants who were not public and manifest heretics; this is a vacant See held by men outside the Body for almost a century which your proposition fail to discern.

"There is no ordinary mission in the Apostasy." Granted. Then do not charge theft of ordinary mission. None was claimed. We are claiming supplied jurisdiction until the situation resolves.

"All titles fell with Vatican II." Granted for those sees. Then those men cannot issue the mandate you demand. A vacant chair does not grant can. 953 (CIC 1917).

"No color of title, therefore rebels." Color of title is a tool for supplied jurisdiction, not the essence of Order. The Holy Council of Trent attached validity to matter, form and intention. As the mandate is a form of catholic disciplinary law, loss of office does not erase the character of orders.

"Epikeia against the Primacy is heresy." False for a manifest and public heretic (1) cannot be elected pope and (2) cannot be the Roman Pontiff since (3) heretics cannot have juridi. The dogma of Papal Primacy is Peter’s perpetual office. That office gives supremam et
plenam potestatem iurisdictionis to the legitimate succesors of the Prince of the Apostle. It is not some disciplinary law still binding as if a Catholic pope were applying it. Necessity does not create a rival pope. It prevents a purely ecclesiastical norm from extinguishing the hierarchy divine law instituted.

"Title alone guarantees mission from the Holy See." Title guarantees ordinary jurisdiction when the Holy See is in Catholic hands. In a ordinary scenario, that is absolutelly true, but we are living in a prolongued vacancy againsy the Papacy itself. Indefectibility then requires the Church to supply what the vacant See cannot give, and bishops in possession of Order to act so that a true pope can one day be restored. 

S. Jerome names desolation in the temple, and the Saint is absolutelly right. He does not define that Catholics must let Order die until the consummation.

Heresy, schism and apostasy sever from the Body: a public heretic is not a member, can. 188 §4 vacates the office, and a vacant See gives no ordinary jurisdiction.

The 1968 rites do not fill that void; where form and intention are altered they do not make Catholic bishops nor priests. 

The Council Constance is not this case for it was uncertainty among non-heretical claimants, not a succession of men outside the Church who emptied the offices and then changed the rite of Order. 

What indefectibility still requires is the old-rite power of Order in men who belong to the Body, with jurisdiction supplied for the act, and a council of such bishops: not a second Rome, not mission from dead titles, but the only college of bishops left that can keep the sacrament alive until a true pope exists again.

text:
I met a yogi near the Neelkanth Mahadev Temple, and he taught me one of the best lessons about karma I have ever heard.

While discussing Jyotisha and karma, I asked him a simple question: “What is the true meaning of karma?”

In a very humble way, he replied, “Karma is a very complex subject. Perhaps it is one of the hardest and deepest subjects to discuss, and I don’t have the authority to define it completely.”

But then he said something that stayed with me. 

“Your intention is the primary thing. What you think and why you perform an action matters the most.”

He explained that you may perform something that appears positive and good, but if your intention behind it is wrong, that action can eventually harm you. On the other hand, an action may appear unpleasant or negative to someone, but if your intention is pure, it can ultimately help you.

Then he gave me a beautiful example.

Suppose someone is unwell and you give them a very bitter medicine. They may dislike the taste, become angry with you, or even curse you for making them take it. But your intention is to make them healthy. The bitterness is temporary; the purpose behind the action is positive.

Now imagine giving someone a very pleasant and delicious dish, knowing that it is poisonous. They may enjoy it, appreciate you for it, and think you have done something good for them. But if your intention is to harm them, the karma behind that action is completely different.

We discussed many other subjects that day, but this was the one lesson that stayed with me.

Karma is not always about how an action appears from the outside. Sometimes, the real weight of an action lies in the intention behind it. That is why, no matter what you do, always try to keep your intention pure and positive.

Perhaps this is what makes karma so subtle. We can control our actions to some extent, but the real test is what is happening within us while we perform them. The world may judge us by what it sees, but karma sees the intention behind it. So before asking whether an action is right or wrong, perhaps we should first ask ourselves: “Why am I doing this?” If the intention is pure, sincere, and free from the desire to harm, we are already walking in the right direction.

text:
Odyssey 
A Spoiler-Filled Analysis for Those Who Are Yet To Sail

This is not a review for the uninitiated. If you have not yet seen Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, or if you've never wrestled with Homer’s original epic, turn back now. We are not discussing whether the IMAX sequences are breathtaking (they are) or if Matt Damon’s Odysseus carries the weary gravitas of a man who has outlived his own Gods (he does). Instead, we are here to dissect the ghost Nolan has smuggled into the hull of this classic retelling. It's a contemporary analogue so specific to 2026 that it feels less like subtext and more like a live cautionary tale embedded into an ancient myth.

Nolan has always played with time, but in Odyssey, he plays very cleverly with the repetition of history using the theme of imperial collapse. The whole team did a great job selling the movie and while the marketing promised a faithful retelling of the Iliad and its aftermath, the film is secretly about something far more uncomfortable. It's the slow, self-inflicted implosion of Western imperialism, viewed through the dual lenses of two historical moments. The sacking of Troy and the destruction of the twin towers.

The Gift Horse That Broke the Imperial Moral Code

The film’s centrepiece is not the journey home, but the memory of the fall. When Odysseus recounts the sacking of Troy to Penelope, Nolan does something audacious. He frames the Trojan Horse not as a clever ruse, but as an act of sacred self-betrayal. In the moral logic of the ancient world, a gift offered to a city under siege carried a curse for all those associated. By hiding destruction inside that gift, the Greeks didn’t just find a way behind the city walls, they shattered their own moral and legal foundation. They won the war, but they destroyed the very code for living and their sacred covenant with the Gods which defined their civilisation.

Nolan’s visual language leaves no room for ambiguity. As Troy burns, the towers of Ilion collapse straight into their own footprints. The camera lingers on the jagged beams of the palace jutting from the blazing rubble, dust plumes billowing horizontally through narrow streets. These images could be read as stylistic homages to disaster films. But they are in fact deliberate visual references to the destruction on 9/11. The smoking crater where the Trojan tower once stood is the smoking pit of Ground Zero. Nolan is drawing a stark comparison, the fall of Troy is, in his telling, the fall of the Twin Towers. The sacking of Troy is not, as the songs suggest, a great victory for Agamemnon and Odysseus. Odysseus presents the event as a tragedy inflicted on Greece from within, a symptom of internal rot. The parallels with 9/11 here are solid. The songs tell us it was 22 Saudi jihadists attacking the imperial core from outside because they hate freedom.

The film invites this reading precisely because the reality of what happened is still unknown. The 9/11 commission was a whitewash and all the important questions remain unanswered. Why did the structures collapse in such a fashion? Why was NORAD unresponsive? If two of the hijackers were recruits of US and Saudi Intelligence, why did the authorities not know the attack was coming? What happened to Building Seven? Was it a controlled demolition?
